speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. In light of the fact that a majority of the aviation community has brought air traffic movements to a halt in Canada on
Oral Questions
the grounds that it is not safe to fly in present circumstances, and noting that the Minister of Transport has promised an inquiry into the implications for safety of the possible introduction of bilingual air traffic procedures which were to be conducted simultaneously with the MOT simulator study, can the Prime Minister tell us when a commissioner is to be named to conduct this inquiry?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: DATE OF APPOINTMENT OF COMMISSIONER TO INVESTIGATE SAFETY OF BILINGUAL TRAFFIC CONTROL-REASON FOR DELAY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the search for a commissioner or commissioners to replace the one who resigned recently is actively going on and we hope to be able to name a commissioner very soon. I would point out that the work in which that commission would have to engage would probably take a period of several months and it is hoped that the pilots and air traffic controllers will await the outcome of that study. This being the case, I find it very regrettable that some of them would be engaged in a strike because the strike in itself cannot advance the very basic requirements of the commission's work which would be to see how safety could be maintained in every way and be made compatible with the bilingual capacity.

subsubtopic: DATE OF APPOINTMENT OF COMMISSIONER TO INVESTIGATE SAFETY OF BILINGUAL TRAFFIC CONTROL-REASON FOR DELAY
speechtext: My supplementary question is directed to the Acting Minister of Transport or to the parliamentary secretary. In light of the fact that approximately two weeks ago the Minister of Transport requested from the air traffic controllers suggestions as to names for people who could satisfactorily be commissioner or commissioners, could there be some explanation of why there has been a delay and whether official communications have been concluded with the air traffic controllers to say whether or not the proposals they have put forward are acceptable.

subsubtopic: DATE OF APPOINTMENT OF COMMISSIONER TO INVESTIGATE SAFETY OF BILINGUAL TRAFFIC CONTROL-REASON FOR DELAY

As the hon. gentleman will appreciate, the job which the commissioner or commissioners will have to do is extremely important and one that requires substantial expertise and sensitivity to the issues that are involved. Therefore, it is our hope that we will be able to find the best person possible to conduct that inquiry, so we are conducting the broadest possible search in order to find the individual or individuals who will do the job that is necessary.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Minister of Transport who, I understand, is attending the funeral of his father-and all hon. members extend their sincerest sympathy and condolences-I would like to ask the Prime Minister whether the government would be willing to widen the terms of reference of the commission of inquiry to include not only the matter of bilingualism in air traffic control, but also the adequacy of equipment which air traffic controllers have to use at airports generally in Canada, and their working

conditions, in the light of the kind of stress they have to work under in present circumstances.

They are, of course, of interest to the government, and the parliamentary secretary indicated just last Thursday or Friday that if there were anything particular that the government should do to increase safety by way of instruments, it would gladly hear any representations, of the hon. member or of anyone else.

subsubtopic: INQUIRY WHETHER DAIRY POLICY WILL BE MODIFIED AND WHEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Agriculture.
The Quebec Order of Agronomists analyzed the new dairy policy of the federal government last weekend and underlined the serious consequences which are already being felt in this area, namely the sale of major farm equipment which is close to zero and the decline of 50 per cent in the sale of feeds.
Considering that industrial milk producers have really agreed to lower their production in the last two months, can the minister tell the House whether his department proposes to change the dairy policy enunciated a few months ago and when.

speakeroldname: Hon. E. F. Whelan (Minister of Agriculture):
subsubtopic: INQUIRY WHETHER DAIRY POLICY WILL BE MODIFIED AND WHEN
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, over a week ago we announced what we were considering at that time whether any changes were to be made in the policy. I would remind the hon. member that the dairy policy was agreed to by the dairy farmers of Canada. The dairy farmers of Canada will have to agree to any new conditions in the dairy policy. It will not be without any discussion with them if changes are to be made. This is an agreement signed by the dairy farmers of Canada and the provinces. The real problem is the distribution of quotas within the provinces themselves. If the provincial people would quit passing the buck to Ottawa, it would be better for all producers concerned.

PROPOSED INTRODUCTION OF QUOTAS ON TEXTILE IMPORTS-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce. As the United States retains 90 per cent of its domestic textile market for its own producers, the European Economic Community retains 80 per cent and Canada retains only 46 per cent, is the government planning to introduce quotas on textile imports which will more closely approach those of our most important trading partners and thereby make it unnecessary for
Oral Questions
the large scale and steadily increasing lay-offs and closing of plants which have been taking place in recent months in the Canadian textile industry, due to a steadily increasing stream of cheap imports from law wage countries?

subtopic: PROPOSED INTRODUCTION OF QUOTAS ON TEXTILE IMPORTS-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald C. Jamieson (Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subtopic: PROPOSED INTRODUCTION OF QUOTAS ON TEXTILE IMPORTS-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it was only last week that there was full and detailed debate on this subject in this House. I answered many of the questions at that time. I can assure the hon. gentleman I used the words "more quotas" than at the present time because we have quotas on a great number of commodities and textiles. We are presently considering additional ones relating to such things as outerwear. As I told the House during the debate last week there is an industry, government and provincial committee with labour representation on it which is asked to report to me by the end of this month the further steps that should be taken.

subtopic: PROPOSED INTRODUCTION OF QUOTAS ON TEXTILE IMPORTS-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. As the minister stayed very clearly away from this issue of increased quotas in his speech in the House last week, and as those people in the industry with whom he has been dealing and will be meeting later on are unanimously and strongly of the opinion that the only way to correct this disastrous and increasingly serious situation is to increase quotas to levels more approaching those imposed by the European Economic Community and the United States, I again ask the minister if he will give serious consideration to bringing Canadian quotas to a level closer to those of the countries with which we deal on a larger scale, the United States and the European Economic Community, so that this industry, which is in very serious condition right now and is getting worse day by day, will not perish?

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subtopic: PROPOSED INTRODUCTION OF QUOTAS ON TEXTILE IMPORTS-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as I said in my comments the other day we are looking at whether there should be a different arrangement of quotas or an expansion of the quota system. The hon. member says it is the unanimous view that this will solve the problem. I would say to him that there are certain sectors that are by no means of that view. There is a certain degree of conflict which we are seeking to eliminate at the present time. I have indicated that we are flexible and that if some proposals come forward that make sense and would bring about the result that the hon. member desires, and which we all desire, we certainly would look at it very seriously and quickly.

speechtext:
That this House condemns the government for its cynical behaviour at the Habitat conference held recently in Vancouver, first, in its
June 21, 1976

position on land speculation; second, its policy of placing commercial criteria ahead of any others in the sale of nuclear reactors; and third, the obvious conflict between the government's bold statements on such environmental matters as clean water and its inability or unwillingness to enforce minimal standards in Canada, as in the case of the Great Canadian Oil Sands plant in northern Alberta.
He said; Mr. Speaker, the motion today refers to the recent United Nations conference in Vancouver on human settlements which was hosted by Canada and was called Habitat. This conference of over 125 countries, involving 4,000 persons, was a follow-up to the UN conference held in Stockholm on the environment, the conference in Rome on food, the conference in Belgrade on population, and the conference in Mexico on the status of women. Hon. members will note that in the motion I am critical of the performance of the government of Canada. It was outvoted, outclassed and outmanoeuvered, and played a role of compromise, cajoling, pleading and begging instead of giving leadership and direction to the problems of human settlements.
I am not critical of government ministers who represented Canada. The Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Danson), who acted as president of the conference, is a decent, open, honest and compassionate person-

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF GOVERNMENT FOR ITS ALLEGED CYNICAL BEHAVIOUR AT HABITAT CONFERENCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF GOVERNMENT FOR ITS ALLEGED CYNICAL BEHAVIOUR AT HABITAT CONFERENCE
speechtext:
-who spoke from the heart in the hardfist-ed business of politics. But the head as well as the heart must be used in respect of these problems.
The Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) worked hard and long trying to defend the indefensible and trying to reach compromise solutions. What annoyed many Canadian delegates and observers was the weak and vacillating position of the government on the main issue of land, nuclear reactors, clean water and the new international economic order. I should like to demonstrate the government's poor and pitiful performance. The moral tone of the conference was set by the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Trudeau), Mother Teresa, the Vancouver symposium made up of Barbara Ward and 23 other world-renowned human settlement experts, and the Minister of State for Urban Affairs. I should like members to listen to what the Prime Minister said at the opening of the conference. He said:
Love is all you need-
But ordinary love will not be enough, according to the Prime Minister.
The only type of love which would be effective in the tightly packed world we already live in would be a passionate love-
Then he quoted Teilhard and said:
Love one another, or you will perish.
Then he said:
Life would become intolerable if one failed to love one's neighbour, the only path is a "conspiracy of love"-in this lies the salvation of human settlements and the hope held forth by Habitat...
The ordinary people, the youth, of whatever age, the participants in the parallel Habitat forum-all have a commitment. And of all the factors bearing down on the conference, Trudeau stressed that urgency was as important as any.
The long years of experience, the specialization, the advanced knowledge and the wisdom of the delegates of Habitat, mixed with the imagination, the originality, the spontaneity, the boldness and the
Habitat Conference
irreverence to be found at Habitat forum will produce, I am sure, an effervescence of quality.
That is what the Prime Minister said at the opening of the conference to set the moral tone. Let me relate what Mother Teresa had to say. Mother Teresa, the saint from the Calcutta slums, told people at the Habitat forum to put their love into living action and to give love until it hurts. She said:
Let us not just put this love into words. Let us love until it hurts.
Mother Teresa responded to the words of the Prime Minister in respect of a conspiracy of love by saying that the Prime Minister of Canada should match his words and his actions in accordance with what he stated at the opening of the conference. The Prime Minister's actions and Canada's actions were deafening by their silence and inaction. The third group to set forth the tone of the conference was the Vancouver symposium lead by Barbara Ward and 23 other renowed human settlement experts. The following is a news release:
The Vancouver conference is about the whole of life, says the declaration. "It is in settlements that mankind achieves happiness, justice and dignity-or suffers rejection, despair and deepening violence-Let Vancouver be remembered as a city where a new hope was born".
Then they set forth some of the problems which we are facing in respect of human settlements, and offered some solutions. They said that every encouragement must be given to the citizens themselves to arrange, build and diversify their communities. The declaration contains a strong commitment to public control over development land. The unearned increment created by changes in land use must return to the community, the 24 experts said, and not to private land owners. They also propose a moratorium on nuclear power and the transfer of research and resources to income-energy systems like solar power. The fantastic waste of resources and energy in western technologies, the declaration states, are errors and extravagances which all countries, developed and developing alike, can and should avoid. This was the statement led by Barbara Ward, Margaret Mead, Buckminster Fuller and others who set forth the moral tone.
May I relate what the Minister of State for Urban Affairs said. I quote from the Vancouver Province:
Danson said the ultimate reason for poverty is not a lack of resources but a lack of political will. "We have an opportunity here to change that choice. This, to me, is what we mean when we speak of Habitat as a solution-oriented conference."
Danson later held his first news conference as Habitat president. He repeated the position that industrialized nations must increasingly share their wealth with the developing world.
"If we try to isolate ourselves from other parts of the world, there will be despair and violence and from that we cannot escape, nor should we escape."
May I deal with the performance of Canada with regard to the Habitat conference. Canada's performance was disappointing and duplicitous. It was duplicitous in the sense of pretending to listen, but not acting. Senator Perrault was the embodiment of the duplicity in the sense of being all things to all men. The Prime Minister, on Monday at the opening of the conference, spoke of the conspiracy of love. On Tuesday, the day after, he said that Canada will not stop the sale of nuclear reactors to other countries. On Wednesday, Maurice Strong, the chairman of Petro-Canada took an opposite view and expressed the need for a

June 21, 1976
Habitat Conference
moratorium to study the impact and safeguards with regard to nuclear reactors. You could hear and feel the crash of the moral tone as a result of the statement by the Prime Minister with regard to a moratorium on nuclear reactors.
Second, with regard to the land issue, the conference started off with the principle that unearned increment should be returned to the community. Canada played the role of compromise, the role of waffling and vacillating with regard to the particular course Canada should accept. Mr. Speaker, this begged the question of how much of the unearned profits should be returned to the community. Should it be 5 per cent, 10 per cent, 95 per cent, or 100 per cent? The Minister of Justice summed it all up to the delegates. He said that this is a political question to be determined by the particular government. The final draft read:
The unearned increment resulting from the rise in land values resulting from change in use of land, from public investment or decision, or due to the general growth of the community, must be subject to appropriate recapture-
Again it begged the question: What is appropriate recapture. Is it 5 per cent, is it 10 per cent, or is it 100 per cent? The problem with regard to the recapture of unearned profits was a problem that Canada had because it was in the grips of the land developers. It was in the grips of William Teron, the president of CMHC. It was in the grips of Keith Morley, the president of Costain Land Development Company, and it was in the grips of the minister of housing for Alberta, William Yurko. It was they, and they alone, who set the vacillating and compromising position of Canada which Canada took with regard to the recovery of unearned profits relating to land. I shudder to think what would have happened to Canada's position if the persons representing the non-governmental organizations had not applied pressure to the delegates and the ministers concerning this problem.
The third issue is that of clean water. Practically every country there agreed on the general principle that we should have clean water either by 1986 or 1990. Clean water should be available by those dates to all persons throughout the world. What did Canada do? Canada did not make any dollar commitment to implement this principle. The best Canada could do was to have one of their delegates from the Department of Finance, Brian Hunter, come to the NGO meeting and say, "Really, gentlemen, this falls under CIDA. We have $1 billion to spend under CIDA, and perhaps we can spare $70 million to $100 million under this program. But really it is up to the developing countries to determine whether they want this money." If Canada had wanted to show leadership and direction, they would have said that we have money available immediately outside CIDA to implement this program. Then they would have had the support and encouragement of all the other countries. But no, they vacillated, they compromised, they refused to act.
The other area was with regard to the new international economic order which would have taken care of monetary reform, trade patterns, resource development and multinationals, because all these have formed part of the problems of human settlements. The answer of the Canadian govern-

ment was that they could not discuss this because the problems had already been discussed at the other UN conference of UNCTAD and therefore Canada could not disturb what took place there. You can see the position of refusing to act on a moratorium concerning nuclear reactors. There was waffling and compromising with regard to land, no action with regard to international economic order, and no dollar commitment with regard to clean water. Is it any wonder that Canada's performance was disappointing and duplicitous?
The real performers at the conference were the non-governmental organizations which were represented by approximately 200 persons. They were chaired by Mark Dorfman and the co-ordinator was Bernard Daly. It was they alone who had a real appreciation of the problems of human settlements, and it was they alone who forced the government to take the small steps that it took. I should like to read from the resolutions that the NGOs put forth to this government. I will summarize them because they are rather lengthy. In the Canadian NGO manifesto they said the following regarding the new international economic order:
1.	Regarding the new international economic order, let Canada take action to lead in establishing new international agreements and arrangements regarding trade, monetary systems, industrial strategies and resource development programs that are advantageous to the developing countries. Let Canada's response to the needs of poor countries not be only aid through the Canadian International Development Agency (CIDA).
2.	Let land be treated as a community resource and not as a market commodity ...
3.	Let Canada lead in establishing a moratorium on expansion of nuclear power, with accompanying emphasis on alternative power sources and on energy conservation.
4.	Let there be an end to fragmentation of housing programs among the federal, provincial and municipal levels of government. Let priority in housing be directed to special-need groups, especially by means of government action at all levels to control the cost of land and the cost of money for housing.
5.	Let there be a Canadian dollar commitment now to programs for clean water ...
6.	Let indigenous land claims be settled prior to the undertaking of development projects in Canada; and let special attention be paid to advancing the equality of indigenous women and to the general needs of native peoples in such matters as housing and jobs . ..
8. Let there soon be right to information legislation covering all levels of government in Canada.
They also added to that the need to develop a conservation-oriented society. This is what the Canadian position should have been, and what the Canadian delegates should have expressed at the conference. If they had, they would have had a splendid response, not only in Canada but throughout the world. The least that can be done now is for the Minister of Justice and the Minister of State for Urban Affairs to meet at a post-Habitat conference in Canada with the representatives of the non-governmental organizations and address themselves to the answers to the problems and to the solutions that they set forth to the government.
One of the main problems-and I dealt with it in a way- was the problem of land. Canada's position with regard to land and to the United Nations reveals a weakness at the federal, provincial and municipal levels. The high cost of housing in Canada is made up of three components: the cost of materials, the cost of financing, and the cost of land.
June 21, 1976

We in the NDP have pointed out to the minister on many occasions that the high cost with regard to financing is due to the fact that mortgages are in the control of the financial institutions which control the flow of moneys and determine the interest rates. Is it any wonder that people in Canada today are paying between 11.5 per cent and 12 per cent for mortgages? It is because the control and flow of mortgage money is in the hands of the financial institutions instead of under the control of the government.
The control of land for housing in Canada is in the hands of developers, and the government aids and abets the developers and speculators to increase their profits at the expense of home buyers. When I heard the Minister of Justice, the developers and the minister of housing for Alberta, Mr. Yurko, speak with regard to the recovery of unearned profits on land, I heard them say that in Canada they can recapture these unearned profits through the capital gains tax, the special speculation taxes in certain provinces, the corporation taxes, the municipal taxes and the impost taxes with regard to services. All these instruments do not work, and land developers are gouging the purchasers by unwarranted, unjustified and unconscionable profits in land development. They are treating land as a commodity instead of a community resource.
This philosophy is expressed by the developers and they are aided and abetted by the government. Back in 1973 this government commissioned Peter Spurr to make a special study with regard to the land problems across Canada. He prepared a report and gave it to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. CMHC did not publish it for public use, but James Lorimer, who is a specialist in urban affairs, a teacher, writer and publisher, published the work of Peter Spurr with regard to land. The real thrust of his report is that in all the main cities across Canada, with the present exception of Montreal, land for housing purposes is in the hands of small groups of developers who make enormous profits and who pay little or no taxes on these profits because of the tax laws with regard to capital cost allowances, and the accounting and reporting procedures of these land development companies.
This is the price the Minister of State for Urban Affairs has had to pay to accomplish an increase in housing starts across the country. He had to give to the developers all the tax advantages available to them. This is the rip-off to which home buyers in Canada have been subjected to obtain shelter.
Let me deal with two examples. Let me deal, first, with the example which was raised by Wendy Day on CTV this past week when she said that in Erindale, Mississauga, in 1972 a three-bedroom bungalow on a 50-foot lot cost $32,850. To qualify, a purchaser required an annual income of $12,000. A down payment of $9,000 was made, which the purchaser obtained from the sale of his former home. With the down payment of $9,000 and a mortgage of $25,000 at 83/4 per cent interest, the monthly payment for principal and interest amounted to $204.96; with taxes, $270 a month. Today, less than four years later, the same bungalow two miles away, situated in Erindale, Mississauga, costs $63,995. That is almost a 100 per cent increase.
Habitat Conference
The purchaser now requires an income of over $20,000, and with a down payment of $15,500 and a mortgage of $48,480 at 11 per cent, the payments are now $466.83 for principal and interest; and with taxes included, $530 a month. That dramatizes how the cost of homes has increased in the short period from 1972 to 1976. In 1972, 50-foot lot in Mississauga cost $12,850. That same lot, in 1976, sells for $30,934, 2l/i times the price of 1972. This situation with regard to Erindale is true of all the major cities in Canada.
In an article by James Lorimer published in the Globe and Mail of May 22 he pointed out that in 1972 in Calgary a three-bedroom home on a 50-foot lot cost $25,000. In 1976 the same home on a 40-foot lot costs $54,000, an increase of more than 100 per cent; and an income of over $21,600 is required. In 1972, the average 50-foot lot in Calgary cost $6,320. In 1976 it costs $20,400, three times as high. Mr. Lorimer points out that the largest Canadian development corporations are in the land banking and land development business on a very big scale indeed.
Information collected by Peter Spurr for 1973 showed a total of 119,192 acres owned by 47 development corporations in about 21 Canadian cities. These private land banks in many instances are large enough to supply all the new land required for housing for the next five years. I am going to repeat that: these companies have enough land within their control to supply all the housing needs of Canada for the next five years. Around Ottawa and Hull- and I am sure the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Gauthier) will be interested in this-nine corporations were found to own 9,416 acres. That is almost 15 square miles of land. It is an eight-year supply at current new house densities and projected growth rates. Around Toronto, 24 firms were listed as owning 41,198 acres, and nine large firms held 87 per cent of that land. The same pattern prevails across the country with regard to the control of land by the development companies and with regard to the cost, profiteering and release of that land.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF GOVERNMENT FOR ITS ALLEGED CYNICAL BEHAVIOUR AT HABITAT CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, like the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Gilbert), I, too, have some critical comments to make about the government's performance at Habitat. I want to begin on a positive note, however, by congratulating the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Danson) not only for his chairmanship of the entire conference, where I thought he conducted himself with great dignity and did credit to our whole country, but I want to pay him a particular tribute for his speech on Thursday night at the climactic moment of Habitat. As he, himself, described it, it was a speech from the heart, a speech that I think spoke for many Canadians who saw in Habitat a chance to make a forward move in the whole direction of international development.
Having said that about the minister, Mr. Speaker, I want to ask the House to consider some of the reasons the government's performance was indeed, as the hon. member for Broadview said, so cynical with respect to Habitat- cynical for a much deeper reason than the three mentioned by the previous speaker.
The motion deals with the specifics of land speculation, the spread of nuclear technology, and putting water in settlements, it says that the government was cynical with respect to those three matters. I could agree with that, but I think, despite the lip service that the hon. member for Broadview paid to Barbara Ward, he indicated that he still thought Habitat was fundamentally a housing conference. Habitat was far more than a housing conference, Mr. Speaker. In order to have any kind of realistic evaluation of what it was trying to do, what it failed to do, and why the Canadian government was cynical in its conduct during that conference, Habitat has to be seen in its total perspective.
It is quite true that the press of this country branded Habitat a failure. The press, that paragon of wisdom, reported up and down this country that Habitat was a failure because of the Arab-Jewish enmity which was carried from the halls of the United Nations in New York into the Queen Elizabeth theatre in Vancouver, turning a conference that was designed to provide settlements for people around the world into a prolongation of that terrible conflict in Palestine, and because of the Arab intransigence in insisting that the final declaration of principles contain an oblique derogation of Israel, forcing Canada along with 14 other countries to vote against the declaration. The press has regarded this whole performance as a failure.
That is too superficial a view of what Habitat was. I do not say that Habitat was a success. I deplore as strongly as anyone the ugly Mid-east battle that took place in Vancou-
June 21, 1976

ver, a battle of words, a battle of resolutions, a battle to slow down the very slow progress being made in the area of international development. But to tell the Canadian people that Habitat goes down the drain because of this resolution is to miss the point of what Habitat was. What did Habitat try to tell us, what was it trying to tell the world? Why was it more than just a housing conference?
One third of the entire urban population of the developing world lives in slums and settlements. Thirty per cent do not have water within 100 metres of their home. More than half the people in developing countries do not have electricity. Those are just the opening statements in the description of a world scene in which hundreds of millions of people in the 35 developing countries, now called the fourth world, live under conditions of absolute poverty and deprivation. It forms a global ghetto which closes in on them while pressing out on the rest of the world.
In many small, developing countries where dramatic growth has occurred, the benefits have not reached all the people. Of course, the question of numbers enters into it. The figures of the growth of cities, especially in the third world, are horrendous. Of the 17 cities in the world that are now called the "ten million" cities because they have populations in excess of ten million, ten will shortly be in the developing world where there is a desperate shortage of existing social services to provide the inpouring migrants with a semblance of human dignity. It did not take Habitat to tell us the situation of global disparity which produces this mass poverty.
The United Nations, through the series of conferences of which Habitat was but one, has shown us the global picture. The environment conference of 1972, the population conference, the world food conference of 1974, and the status of women conference in 1975, together with related conferences, culminated in the seventh special session of the United Nations in 1974-75 which gave us the new economic order. These factors, considered together, give us an overview of the global scene today, of which Canada is one part, and show us how serious the situation has become.
The situation has arisen because of the manner in which we and other industrialized nations maintain our standard of living and growth. We do it with the continued acquisition of technology, capital and resources which feed the ever-growing demands of our societies. The problem is terribly complex and can only be resolved by a new international partnership of developed and developing nations. I add, parenthetically, that the days of aid are over. I am talking of aid in the sense that it can raise the standard of living of people trapped in countries without resources, technology and capital. Aid is a "way-station" on the way to true reforms of social and economic systems which will allow the peoples of the underdeveloped countries of the world to become self-reliant. Basically, that is what Habitat was all about. It was concerned with specific questions relating to human settlements.
We should not think, by any means, that the speech of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) at Habitat, and the speech of Mother Teresa, earlier referred to this afternoon, set the tone of Habitat. The previous speaker suggested
Habitat Conference
that the tone of Habitat was set by the Prime Minister of our country and Mother Teresa speaking eloquently and rhetorically about love. That tone was quickly dissipated by the President of Mexico, President Echeverria, in the most under-reported speech of the whole conference. President Echeverria, who headed the delegation from Mexico to Habitat, was given a standing ovation in the plenary hall. He excoriated the industrialized nations for not following their rhetoric of the past few years with action which would help developing nations. I shall quote a paragraph or two of President Echeverria's speech to show the mood of Habitat, a mood to which Canada failed to respond. That led to cynicism. President Echeverria said, in part:
How could the human tide that is moving the cities actually be kept in the rural areas with a decent standard of living when the prices of food and raw materials are at the mercy of mercantile monopolization and iniquitous international speculation? ...
The attitude which the industrial states have recently adopted in economic matters reveals the extent to which their real dispute is waged not in the sphere of worldwide ideological conflict but rather in that of specific economic interests, and how easy it is for powerful minorities to reach circumstantial agreement when the majorities make specific demands and organize for action. When matters come to a head, however, questions of profit and loss have always proved more powerful than the standards of freedom, democracy, justice and solidarity.
The President of Mexico told the world and delegates to Habitat that despite the gravity of conditions facing developing nations, the industrialized world is not backing its sentiments of love with concrete action. It has not adopted the great resolutions previously passed by the United Nations. He specifically referred to the fourth UNCTAD conference which ended in Nairobi a few days before the Habitat conference began. Hon. members will recall that we discussed the work of the conference in this House a little over a week ago. It turned on the validity of the principle of a common fund being established for some ten buttressed commodities which developing nations export and on which they depend for foreign exchange, exchange with which they pay for the manufactured goods and commodities they need.
Although the matter was highly technical, the main line of the argument became clear. It was this: an integrated system to protect the prices of primary commodities produced in developing countries must be in place if those developing countries are to be given a chance at being self-reliant. Canada at the beginning of the UNCTAD conference gave lip service to the idea. At the end of the conference we said we would go along with the establishment of the common fund provided it was actually established. That quasi-commitment was dragged out of Canada in the course of the UNCTAD conference.
I mention the UNCTAD conference while talking of Habitat because both conferences are very much connected. Both Habitat and UNCTAD bear some relationship to the principles set forth in the UN charter of rights dealing with duties of states, and with the new economic order. These matters were raised in the declaration of principles. Canada voted against the declaration of principles which the Habitat conference finally produced. We voted against the declaration for reasons set out by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford), the head of the Canadian delegation, to the effect that the declaration contains an iniquitous section derogatory of Israel. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if only the Canadian government would be consistent with its own announcements, we would be a lot further down the road to development. I am sure the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Danson) knows precisely what I mean. Canada voted against the declaration of principles presumably because it contained the anti-Zionist section. Actually, the declaration contained other points which made Canada uncomfortable and for which we did not want to vote; and as the Minister of Justice himself said during the two weeks, those points gave Canada a great deal of trouble. For instance, may I quote point 14 of the declaration of principles, which reads:
To achieve universal progress in the quality of life, a fair and balanced structure of the economic relations between states has to be promoted. It is therefore essential to implement urgently the new international economic order, based on the declaration and program of action approved by the General Assembly in its sixth special session, and on the charter of economic rights and duties of states.
If hon. members wish to know in more detail Canada's difficulties with that resolution, I direct their attention to an article written Mr. Bernard Daly in the Ottawa Journal of Friday, June 18 last. He points out that the intransigent position of the Arabs provided a smokescreen behind which Canada was able to hide its opposition to some of the bitter facts which developing nations were including in the declaration of principles. A balanced structure of economic relations between status has to be promoted, yet Canada is not ready for that kind of action.
The Minister of the Environment (Mr. Marchand) was interviewed by the press at Habitat. It was widely quoted across Canada. He said that we could not expect Canada to go along with any of these substantial changes because the government would risk electoral defeat. That is to say that the people of Canada and the Minister of the Environment would not support the changes called for in such declarations as the declaration of principles of Habitat because the government would risk electoral defeat. That is a very interesting point indeed. Is that to say that the government's own five-year strategy of international development co-operation that was published before the seventh special session opened last September-a 21-point dimensional strategy, a structural reform that puts it together as our own policy, which I have several times said in this

House that I support-will not be implemented because the government is afraid of electoral defeat?
Let us follow this down to hard specifics. I know the Minister of State for Urban Affairs is extremely familiar with this. I quote from our mutual friend, Barbara Ward, who wound up her brilliant and masterful book, "The Home of Man", which was the overview of the Habitat situation, by asking: What is it we are really trying to bring about in these structural changes? I quote:
A sustained determination to end hunger in the next ten years-
Is the government afraid of electoral defeat for trying to do that?
-a committed plan to provide every human being with clean water by the mid-eighties-
Will that plan throw the government out of office?
-a strategy for decent shelter for every family as the new century dawns-
Is that program going to defeat any Canadian government? I say that any Canadian government afraid to implement such a program is not worthy of holding office.
The remarks of the Minister of the Environment were widely noted by delegates from around the world when they read the Vancouver press. That minister ought to be excoriated by this House for failing to indicate the true Canadian position, a position supported by all sides of this House, for the movement forward of Canada's meaningful participation in international development. That policy is contained in a report to parliament from the subcommittee on international development, representing all parties, which studies this issue extensively.

I quote:

Canadian influence must not be overestimated, but neither must it be underrated. That is just an inkling of the words that are found in that policy. However, Mr. Speaker, the problem gets down to this very simple reason about which the Minister of the Environment is concerned regarding electoral defeat, namely, that the Canadian people do not know what is going on; they have not been told about this policy.
June 21, 1976

We are debating Habitat this afternoon on an opposition day motion. We debated UNCTAD on an opposition day. We are always doing this. Why does the government not bring in its own motions, resolutions and legislation in order to state in this House its position in a positive way so that we can respond positively? It is wrong for parliament to be debating international development in the context of an opposition day. The government must become committed to promoting its own policy. Do not tell me that they are promoting it. If you go to the shelves of the CIDA library you will find 25,000 copies of the government's five-year strategy, unused and uncirculated. What is wrong with a government that allows its own policy to sit on the shelves?
There is a lot more to be said. I will not say it because my colleagues will speak on some of the specifics with regard to land speculation and the nuclear and water sections of the NDP motion. However, as the first speaker for our side I would be remiss if I did not attempt to point out the true reasons for Canadian government cynicism at Habitat. We went there with an excellent delegation, good leadership and a terrific program brought out by the NGO participation group throughout the country in the preceding year.
Talk about information overload! There was so much good material that even an expert could not absorb it all. There was no reason for the Canadian government not to seize the moment of leadership. UNCTAD centered around a common fund. Habitat centered around the provision of clean water for every human being by 1990. Canada did not stand up and say, "Yes, we will live up to this with a dollar commitment." During the course of Habitat, the Prime Minister said in the House that we are giving money to regular CIDA programs; nothing more special needs to be done. The Minister of State for Urban Affairs knows as well as I do that there was a moment lost at Habitat because we did not live up to our words. That was the true cynicism.
We covered our reluctance to move ahead with the declaration of principles to join in what could have been a consensus. We covered by hiding under the smoke screen of Arab-Israeli resolutions which I deplore. These are terribly complex plans. The United Nations is in great danger of losing the dwindling support it has in the western world. Read the letters to the editor in last Saturday's Toronto Star and you will get the mood of the Canadian people with regard to the UN following the Habitat conference.
The government has a terrific obligation to promote its own policy. That policy is incorporated into its five-year strategy. It centres around industrial co-operation, transfer of technology, trade liberalization and a better pricing policy for the commodities of the world. That is the true way to help the developing nations. The government has a great responsibility to promote that policy and show how it plugs into the United Nations systems of conferences, of which Habitat was one, and how all of that relates to the provisions of the new order. That is the way we are going to make progress.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Mac-Eachen) is co-chairman of the continuing conference of international economic co-operation, the conference of rich
Habitat Conference
and poor producing and consuming nations that meets in Paris. If he is going to maintain his credibility, he will have to be backed up by a government that is willing to move to show the Canadian people the tremendous responsibility we have, and also the opportunity. This is the most important moment in Canadian history because we can move ahead in the global community in which we live by a profound, positive policy of enlightened internationalism.

speechtext:
In my judgment, Habitat will produce lasting improvements. Our experience in Canada indicates a much greater public awareness of the issues which must form part of human settlement policies, and a greater acceptance by all levels of government that these issues must be handled in a comprehensive manner, with full co-operation among the various jurisdictions involved.
In passing, may I say that we seem to have difficulty in Canada with the word "national". We define it as "a confederation", and recognize it has both a federal and a provincial definition. In preparing for and participating in Habitat, we have had to stand back and take a good look at ourselves, our settlements policies and institutions, and consider our values and our hopes for the settlements in which we must live. This process involved not only the federal government but also the governments of the provinces, municipalities, public groups, business and private citizens. Much of this consideration went into Canada's national report to Habitat entitled "Human Settlement in Canada," and into the three short films which we prepared for the conference.
This wide participation was reflected in the Canadian delegation to Habitat, and I would like to express my thanks to all those who so generously gave of their time and effort to join with the federal government in this fully representative delegation. I think that all will agree that the experience has been beneficial in itself and has set the stage for further co-operation among those concerned with settlements in Canada. From our observation at the conference, it seemed clear that many other nations had similar beneficial experiences in preparing for, and participating in, Habitat, and that we may expect that all nations, separately and jointly, will be approaching the problems of human settlements in a more coherent manner and with a greater sense of urgency.
Canada's objectives at Vancouver were twofold. First, as host government we were responsible for providing the extensive facilities and services required for such a conference and for the parallel, non-governmental meeting, the Habitat forum. I can report that our host arrangements, with the single exception of the weather, met with universal praise and were a credit internationally to Canada, to the province of British Columbia and to the city of Vancouver. In addition to the usual conference facilities, we provided extensive facilities for television coverage and for the use of audio-visual presentations, and many of these new techniques will undoubtedly be incorporated into future world conferences as a result of their effectiveness in Vancouver.
We were a participant in the Habitat conference, as well as host, and we took a very active role and received from every member a full measure of co-operation. We put forward a clear and balanced view of our national settlements policies and tested these policies in discussions with other nations. We have learned a good deal about what is happening in other nations, some of which will undoubtedly find its way into our own practices and will show us how best we may assist other nations who will require considerable outside assistance in improving the lives of their people.

In this last regard, I believe that the conference has provided an important new focus for development efforts, a focus on the place and the manner in which people live, rather than some impersonal objective such as GNP or tons of metal ingots. The message of Habitat has been that we must address ourselves more directly to the improvement of the life of the individual if we are to improve the lot of the whole. It is for this reason that the Canadian delegation repeatedly stressed the need to identify specific targets in matters which directly affect people's daily lives, such as the availability of safe drinking water, and committed ourselves to assist in the achievement of such goals.
There were several other Canadian initiatives at the conference which I would like to mention. The offer of the University of British Columbia, supported by the federal government and the government of British Columbia, to house a continuing United Nations audio-visual library on human settlements was well received by the conference. Arrangements for this program are now being completed between the university and the United Nations and it is expected that the library will commence operation within a few weeks.
The delegation also succeeded in putting forward some fairly distinctive Canadian views on policy recommendations dealing with the control and the value of land, the rights of indigenous peoples, nuclear energy, the conservation of resources, and the participation by the public in the formulation and implementation of settlements policies and programs. We were also able to gain acceptance for a more positive approach to the role of environmental policies in settlements planning, rather than the purely negative considerations which have been current. Over all of the recommendations for national action discussed at the conference, we sought minor amendments to make them more applicable to federal states such as Canada.
Debate on international co-operation was divided into discussions of new programs which might be undertaken following Habitat, of how the appropriate section of the United Nations secretariat might be reorganized to deal with increased programs, and on a declaration of principles to be issued by the conference to emphasize the role of settlements policy in national and international affairs. The Canadian contribution to the debate on programs included a general commitment to give favourable consideration to settlements projects within our development assistance programs, and several specific commitments: to create the audio-visual library at the University of British Columbia and to continue and expand our support for a human settlements training program at the Asian Institute of Technology at Bangkok. We also indicated that we would be prepared to participate in similar programs in other regions.
On the reorganization of appropriate United Nations secretariat resources, the Canadian delegation argued for a rationalization of all available resources in a single unit, with headquarters in New York but with its staff and activities deployed as much as possible at the regional level. In a fairly extensive debate emerged a fairly broad consensus on what should be done, but it appeared that many nations were not ready to take decisions on the location of the secretariat headquarters or its precise
June 21, 1976

attachment to the United Nations' framework. This will be the subject of further discussions at the summer session of the UN Economic and Social Council and at this fall's General Assembly.
The discussions on the declaration to be issued by Habitat provided the sharpest division among governments at Habitat. At the end of the first week the group of 77 brought forward an amended version of the original draft declaration, a version which included some greatly expanded references to a new international economic order, and an unacceptable reference which would have linked Zionism to racism. Subsequent negotiations failed to improve these aspects of the draft, and in the end the Canadian delegation, together with many others, was obliged to vote against the declaration as a whole when attempts to obtain a paragraph by paragraph vote proved fruitless. The vote was 89 in favour, 15-including Canada-opposed, with 10 nations abstaining. In explanation of the Canadian vote, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) stated that had it not been for the paragraph which sought to link Zionism with racism, Canada would have been in a position to join in a consensus on the declaration.
The vote on the declaration received a great deal of publicity and I think it is important to keep it in perspective. The objectionable feature which led to our negative vote is a matter of a few words in a lengthy document, most of which we did, and shall continue to, support strongly. While the declaration lacks the weight of consensus, it is nevertheless a valuable statement of some of the basic thoughts which should guide nations in improving the lives of their peoples. In addition, the debates on the declaration and the divisions they produced were largely separated from the main bulk of the conference's work and did not detract from the more positive achievements in other areas.
On the whole, therefore, I think that the Canadian delegation can be proud of the twin roles, as host and as a participant in Habitat, and I think we can be confident that this conference will yield great benefits to all peoples over the years to come.

To finish, Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a few remarks on the results of the conference and the wish of some people who want to quantify everything. It is impossible to measure the results of such a conference quanta-tively. One has to attend it to realize what forces were at play and to really take part in it to understand that it is not always possible to reach a consensus by mere good will. It seems utopian to me to quantify the conference in the sense that, for instance, Canada has a national policy to provide clean water to all parts of the country by 1986. A consensus was reached for 1990. We would have preferred it sooner, for all countries. Still, to answer one of the comments made by the opposition, I do not think Canada wants to be paternalistic and impose any programs which might not be well received now in underdeveloped countries.
Problems at the international level, and I think particularly of the terms of the exchange, are acute. The fact remains that, as Mrs. Barbara Ward said, we are dealing with an international problem in which we have the world of the wealthy endowed with a conscience and the world of
Habitat Conference
the poor whose will and force to strike can cause concern. Habitat, Mr. Speaker, may have given us opportunity of becoming aware of the international problem, of exchanging view, of realizing that audio-visual aids are fantastic.
We saw, thanks to electronic devices, what goes on in other countries. For my part, the experience was rewarding. For most of the delegates, it was obviously the experience of a lifetime. I hope the press and hon. members will understand that to quantify the conference in terms of government measures was not the aim of the conference. Its objective was to give an awarenesss of the situation, to give the opportunity to elaborate, to think, to discuss and to exchange views: if the conference has had positive results, I trust they will be given concrete form.
As for speculation, there is a long way to go. The hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Gilbert) said, I know, that we are up against a problem that is difficult to solve. Still the fact remains that the collective will of the people, expressed through the various levels of government, by government representations, in terms of what is a fair profit or gain, will be decided by the governments themselves and not imposed by them, by the government at the top. We have a long way to go, we have a lot to do. Of course, it is important that we should conserve what arable lands we have. We must have overall policies that induce us into conserving them. We must elaborate new policies, as well as new ways and means. I think the minister, in convening his tripartite conferences has found a formula that might work, because town planning is a matter for municipalities and provinces and not the federal government. But I think that to get a group of government bodies in Canada to plan the common good, everyone will have to show considerable good will and recognize the fact that we have not solved all our problems, that we have much to do and that though, in the final analysis, the Habitat Conference may have brought some solutions it did not solve them all. We must continue to work at it.
I conclude, Mr. Speaker, to indicate that the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Danson) will take the floor tonight. He will listen with interest to hon. members' remarks, and I hope those remarks will be positive. In addition, we will have some spokesmen who will discuss certain particular points in the debate, with a view to answering as much as possible hon. members' concerns and questions.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF GOVERNMENT FOR ITS ALLEGED CYNICAL BEHAVIOUR AT HABITAT CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to devote my time this afternoon to the third complaint contained within the NDP motion, that is, the complaint regarding pollution of the Athabasca River from one of the tar sands extraction plants. Just to put this in its proper perspective, I should like to spend a little time on background in so far as the development of tar sands is concerned in a general sense. I believe it is fair to say that this party is every bit as concerned about environmental matters as the author of the motion we are debating, and perhaps even more so than some of the members of his party. But we also want to be realistic and practical in talking about these developments.
We know the Alberta tar sands can produce all the crude oil Canada will need in the foreseeable future if they are developed in an orderly manner. A couple of months ago

June 21, 1976
Habitat Conference
the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie) told the House that Canada is short of oil and gas. I think everybody knows that, and knew it at the time of his statement. He went on to say that the future looked so bad that we would be investing $181 billion in energy projects in this country between now and 1990, and by crossing our fingers the best we could hope for would be limiting our demands on oil imports to one-third of our needs.
I want to question the minister's projections because I think they are not necessarily accurate. We will have to spend on oil exploration and development, according to the minister, $40 billion in 1975 dollars. In return for this massive investment of capital we will increase our productive capacity by 500,000 barrels, or one-third of what the province of Alberta is producing today. But the energy department's own figures and graphs show that development of the Athabasca, Peace River, Wabasca and Cold Lake tar sands would give us the same amount of oil for $6 billion. In fact, the price spread would be still greater because frontier oil has to be carried down from the north in pipelines which are very expensive and, as yet, unbuilt. Pipelines from the tar sands would be shorter and much less costly to construct.
How much oil would we have if we spent $40 billion on new tar sands plants? When it comes on stream in 1978 or 1979, the Syncrude plant at Mildred Lake will produce about 125,000 barrels of synthetic crude oil per day in return for a capital outlay of $2 billion. Other things being equal, it is just simple arithmetic to see that $40 billion would buy us 20 plants with the same productive capacity as Syncrude and would give us 2.5 million barrels of oil per day. Moreover, the civil servants of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie) have been estimating that if world prices for petroleum remain high, close to $6 billion will be spent on tar sands plants without any particular encouragement from the federal government.
The three plants which an additional $6 billion would buy could produce 375,000 barrels of oil per day, bringing total tar sands' production, when Syncrude and Great Canadian Oil Sands are counted in, to over three million barrels per day. As it happens, three million barrels per day is greater than the total Canadian demand for oil is expected to be in 1990. And all this is to say nothing about the enormous savings in pipeline costs which investment in tar sands plants would bring, the very large economies of scale which would come from the building of 20 or more plants, or the tremendous benefits which might accrue to the national economy if Canadian industry were geared to producing the machinery for these plants.
Finally, 20 or 25 tar sands plants would require in excess of 100,000 workers on a permanent basis and would constitute a partial answer to the unemployment from which so many Canadians today are suffering. I am trying to make the point that the development of the Athabasca tar sands, as well as the other three tar sands areas to which I referred earlier, is essential to Canada. Beyond that, I also want to say that Canadians should not expect that Alberta alone should be responsible for developing these plants just to supply energy to the rest of Canada. In other words, there is also a role which the consuming Canadian provinces can play in this development. One of them, Ontario,

already is doing that to some extent in that it is participating in the Syncrude project directly.
However, there are a number of things which need to be done before development takes place in accordance with what I have described as a possibility. Those requirements are that the processed synthetic crude should have access to world prices, as has been guaranteed to Syncrude but so far refused to anyone else who has indicated a desire to develop a plant. The federal government should become less greedy and get away from double-taxation. I realize that greed is one of the government's greatest assets, but I think it should dispose of that asset and get away from the idea of disallowing royalties to be deducted for tax purposes. I think the government should also bring in a program for earlier depreciation write-offs, when we consider, for example, in respect of the Syncrude plant that there is perhaps a $3 billion capital outlay, or between $2 billion and $3 billion, before one single barrel of oil comes out.
Finally, we should consider the tragedy for Canada which would result if the crew of experts, the construction teams, were allowed to disintegrate in 1978 when the construction at Syncrude is finally completed. I think the government should plan that new plants would be started at least as frequently as would be necessary to keep this crew of skilled people assembled and working.
I wanted to put that background material on the record because it emphasizes the proper perspective in respect of pollution control in so far as the plants are concerned. I think the NDP motion complaining about pollution by GCOS originated from a Globe and Mail article of June 9 written by Mary Kate Rowan and entitled "The Athabasca foul-up". In that article there is a suggestion that 400,000 gallons of polluted water is going into the Athabasca River from the tailings pond at the GCOS plant site. This plant and the tar sands happen to be in the middle of my constituency. For that reason alone, if not for any other reason, I usually keep in close contact with the developments in the area. I have been informed by a representative of GCOS that the statement indicating that water from the tailings pond is going into the river is totally erroneous and that indeed there is no polluted water going into the river from the tailings pond.
However, 400,000 gallons of water are going into that river, but they come from a filtering system contained within a large dike built of sand which forms a portion of the wall of the tailings pond. Some tests have been carried on in respect of this effluent. I have a report here which was produced by Environment Canada in September, 1975, concerning this particular problem. I wish to quote from this report because I think it will help clarify the matter before us. The report reads in part:
The liquid effluent being discharged from the effluent holding pond during the sampling period demonstrated no acute toxicity and the chemical parameters measured were all reasonably low. Notably the oil and grease values were low, particularly in comparison to some reported values for this effluent stream. Analysis for metals indicated that all were below detectable limits except for zinc and vanadium. However, the one detectable zinc level was low and could not be considered a problem in relation to other treated industrial effluents. The significance of the vanadium value is uncertain and is currently under investigation by Alberta Environment and Environment Canada. However, it is evident that the vanadium levels present in the effluent did not cause acute toxicity to rainbow trout.
June 21, 1976

There was also some testing carried out with regard to the effluent which comes from the drainage pipes which are the outflow of the filter system I mentioned in the dike forming part of the tailings pond. The effluent from this did contain some toxic materials and the toxicity to rainbow trout was indeed significant. The cause of toxicity could not be conclusively specified from the water chemistry, but the relatively high concentration of total organic carbon and total dissolved solids would likely include the specific compounds or elements responsible for toxicity.
Separation and identification of organic compounds from the organic fraction was shown to be feasible and produced some interesting compound identifications. Further work to comprehensively separate and identify the organic compounds and classes should be pursued under the auspices of the Alberta oilsands environmental research program. I wanted also to read that, because it suggests quite clearly that the industrial people in question are indeed making reasonable efforts to control the pollution.
There has been some toxic effluent from the drainage pipes in the dike. I am informed by this report, as well as by a representative of the industry, that engineering studies are under way which are aimed at collecting this effluent into a collection system of some kind and pouring it back into the settling pond. However, there are some fairly serious problems with that, one of them being that the location of the dike is close to the river and that the collection ponds which might be erected could well be taken away with the spring flow when the river levels are high. That could be a serious problem.
However, I am also informed that tests have been carried out on the river water above, as well as below, the outlet of these pipes and that there was no significant difference in the quantity of the toxic material above and below the outlet from these drainage pipes. The reason for that is that the volume of 400,000 gallons is so small in relationship to the total flow of the river that a substantial dilution of this toxic material takes place immediately, so that the river water is not at all toxic to the fish in it and, indeed, there is an abundant fish supply in the river in that region.
The ratio of this 400,000 gallons to the total river flow is around 3,300-thousands of 1 per cent of the daily river flow or, in other words, .00033 per cent of the total water flowing in the river. This suggests that the volume is so small in relation to the river that there is not much danger. When we compare that to some other areas of pollution right on our doorstep here in Ottawa, we can see that the problem here is much more severe. When the city of Hull pours 10 million gallons of raw sewage a day into the river, and the city of Montreal pours 300 million gallons of raw sewage a day into the St. Lawrence River, we can see that the problem of water pollution much closer to Ottawa than the Athabasca River is substantially greater and, I suggest, perhaps warrants a great deal of immediate attention as well. But for some strange reason our left-wing friends to my left neglected to make any mention of that kind of pollution. I find that rather strange. Of course, I find them a rather strange bunch anyway.

The extremely original statement which we have just heard from the member for Winnipeg North Centre will be duly noted by me. I will see what I can do about it.
I will carry on for a moment because there are a few more things that need to be said about this problem. One of them is that an attack has also been made on Syncrude and GCOS by my friends to the left in so far as the emission of sulphur into the air is concerned. I am told that GCOS is licensed to put out 348 long tons of sulphur, mostly in the form of sulphur-dioxide, and the permit which has been granted Syncrude allows them to put out 287 long tons of sulphur a day. Some reports on this matter have been produced-one of which I have here-again by Environment Canada or the regional department of the environment task force. Through the application of the best available technology, total sulphur emission could be reduced from 287 long tons to an estimated 40 long tons.
I have looked into this problem and I am informed that this equipment to which reference is made is still unproven. Both companies, involved as well as the provincial government, suggest that this equipment is indeed unproven and perhaps not at all practical at this time. I am told also that the use of energy in the operation of a plant with this kind of equipment would be very high and the efficiency of such a plant would be drastically reduced. In addition, no real need has been demonstrated to reduce emissions below that level because studies have been done, again in relation to CGOS which has been operating in the area of 348 long tons a day, and a study was conducted by the Canadian Wildlife Service in 1973, as well as a more recent study in 1975, to determine whether there has been

June 21, 1976
Adjournment Motion
any damage whatsoever to the soil or vegetation within a radius of seven miles around the plant in question-and they all indicated there was no evidence of damage of any sort. So insofar as the Syncrude plant is concerned, it seems difficult to conclude from these two studies that there is a any real need to reduce the emissions beyond the amount granted in the licence.
Finally, in so far as Syncrude is concerned, it is difficult to estimate the cost of installing such equipment. If it were ordered today, I am told it would not be available for another five years, but it may well raise the cost of construction by $1 billion. So we have to consider all these factors before we become too raucous in attacking provincial governments and industry about the decisions which have already been made regarding further development.
I would like to conclude my remarks by stating that I am very concerned that some politicians in this country, and perhaps some other people, are making a lot of unwarranted attacks on the tar sands development. I do not know how much influence that has had upon the federal government, but perhaps it has resulted in a situation where the federal government is turning its attention from the tar sands and is looking to frontier development. According to the figures which I have given, this is a ridiculous decision on their part because such a move is extremely costly and a total gamble. You do not know where or whether you will find the oil, whereas with the tar sands there is no gamble, the development costs less and you wind up with a greater supply of energy for Canada. We are all interested in pollution control but also in self-sufficiency in energy. I would like to suggest that everybody concerned should stop being hysterical about possible errors made in construction associated with the tar sands. We should be very careful to ensure that proper attention is paid to the environment, but we should not be so hysterical as to retard development in that area.
