subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF GOVERNMENT FOR ITS ALLEGED CYNICAL BEHAVIOUR AT HABITAT CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to deal particularly with the clause in the motion which refers to the government's policy of placing commercial criteria ahead of any others in the sale of nuclear reactors. But before I get to that specific subject, I would like to make one or two general remarks.
I do, indeed, support my colleague, the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Gilbert), in his criticism of the government's actions at the Habitat conference, but I want to say that I do not think it follows from that that we wish to criticize the Habitat conference as such. There is too much cynicism about some of these international activities. Of course things happen in international forums which are distasteful to us, but we should not jump from that to saying that the whole thing is a failure. Indeed, to put it mildly, that is premature because it destroys the foundation of the concern and the enthusiasm which is necessary if we are to do the things internationally that the welfare of the people of the world in every country, including Canada, requires.
I do not in any way, by being critical of some of the points of view taken by the government, wish to denigrate the importance or the significance of the conference itself, nor of some of the things the government did.
However, we are an opposition and we look with a critical eye. We frequently find, in the actions of the government, a considerable gap between rhetoric, on the one hand, and action on positive issues on the other. I have been to quite a few international conferences. I have never found a single reason to complain about the rhetoric of the Canadian spokesmen; it has always been of the highest order. But when it came down to practical decisions on practical issues, a different story is told. I want to say to all members of the government that they should try to reconcile their rhetoric with practical actions, and there are many fields where that injunction should be carried out and taken seriously. To get to the question of nuclear reactors, I would like, first, to quote what Albert Einstein said, as follows:
The splitting of the atom has changed everything, save our modes of thinking, and thus we drift toward unparallelled catastrophe.
The subject of nuclear energy which came up at the Habitat conference at Vancouver from time to time is one about which very many serious-minded people in Canada are deeply concerned, but I am afraid the Canadian gov-
June 21, 1976

ernment's action at this conference was inadequate, to put it mildly. There is a fairly new organization called the Canadian Coalition for Nuclear Responsibility. Its supporters include the Primate of the Anglican Church and Moderator of the World Council of Churches, the Very Rev. E. W. Scott; the founder of the Club of Rome, Dr. Aurelio Peccei; and Maurice Strong, president of Petro-Canada, who is well known for his deep concern about these subjects. They have joined others in signing a petition asking for an inquiry into the whole nuclear field. The petition has been signed by General Burns, who is well known not only as a soldier but as a statesman, who is the former head of the U.N. peacekeeping force; a gentleman named Joe Clark, who I believe is known to some hon. members in this House; Alex Campbell, who is Premier of Prince Edward Island; and Gerry Regan, Premier of Nova Scotia, among many others.
This petition deals primarily with the question of the increased reliance on nuclear energy to deal with our energy crisis. The pamphlet which the coalition put out says that the government expects to see 112 CANDU reactors in operation in Canada by the end of the century. The pamphlet goes on to point out that the industry has been exempted from having to carry full accident insurance because no insurance company will risk issuing such a policy. The coalition points out that the inhalation of dust particles and radioactive gases in mines has caused 450 cases of silicosis and/or cancer in Canadian uranium miners. That is something which could have been prevented if the proper controls had been adopted.
The coalition to which I have referred calls for complete public accountability on the subject of nuclear energy, accompanied by a full disclosure of all pertinent information, and as a possible mechanism for realizing these objectives the coalition is challenging the federal government to conduct a public inquiry into all aspects of nuclear power development in this country. I ask the House to note that this refers to all nuclear power development, not just nuclear power for reactors for export but the nuclear power which is going to be used to supplement our energy resources. The coalition says that the proposed inquiry would investigate a host of unanswered questions about the Canadian nuclear program, questions of safety, economics, energy requirements, social impact, health and pollution and the decision-making process itself.
In speaking to this motion I would like to take this opportunity to urge upon the government, as has been done before in this House, that it proceed with such a public inquiry so that the very grave disquiet which many informed people feel on this subject can be allayed by the disclosure of the facts or by the necessary action to prevent these developments.
At the Habitat Conference the question divided itself into two parts. One was about the increased demand, domestically, for the production of nuclear power, and the other was the sale of nuclear reactors abroad. I wish to deal with them separately. I believe the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) addressed himself at the conference to these matters and was very explicit. He said that it is the Canadian government's policy to proceed with the sale of nuclear reactors on a commercial basis, and he linked that with the need for the development of developing countries.
Habitat Conference
I want to challenge the Prime Minister on the suggestion that the developing countries are seeking nuclear reactors, on the whole, for the purpose of developing power. I want to point out what was said at the conference by Mr. Arjaun Makhijani, who works on practical energy solutions in a village near Bombay, which certainly is a part of the world which is underdeveloped. He attacked the policy of imposing large-scale energy projects like nuclear power plants on societies which are not suited for such schemes. Mr. Makhijani said that it is not a question of emotionalism but that nuclear energy is extremely capital-intensive. It must be used 80 per cent of the time in order to be economically efficient, and in the underdeveloped countries it could be used only about 40 per cent of the time, and in villages only about 10 per cent of the time. Because the highly centralized nuclear energy must be used in such an intensive way, it is unsuitable to types of societies, to the underdeveloped countries and to their mainly rural village populations, he said. He went on to say that we could save enough power to deal with this much better and much more cheaply by other methods. He said he rejects, on behalf of developing countries, the theory that the nuclear option is the one that will really solve their problems-problems which not only require scientific developments but require labour-intensive developments to give employment in the countries concerned.
The Prime Minister started out at the conference with what I think must have been a cold douche for the enthusiasts thereby reiterating Canada's stand and basing it on what I suggest is the false belief that this is the best way to help developing nations.
This matter was raised at the NGO conference forum, and was raised again by the group led by Barbara Ward-I think they called themselves the Vancouver symposium- and it was raised in the final conference resolution which, when dealing with the subject of shelter, infrastructure and many other things, recommended an extreme examination of the whole question of energy. An effort was made to add to that the special consideration for hazardous developments in this field and they sought to be put in the words "for example, nuclear power" as a main example of the type of development that was hazardous and ought to be examined. It is my understanding that the Canadian government did not support that, and that the official resolution had no reference to nuclear power. I say they were failing to give the leadership that this country could give and should give in this field.
I should like to turn to the subject of the sale of nuclear reactors. It has been fully debated in this House a number of times, so there is not much point in repeating what has been said at length. I believe the three opposition parties joined in a motion criticizing the government for the sale of nuclear reactors to certain countries and urged that we stop this particular policy. The government responded by saying that sales would continue on the grounds that we had safeguards.
Mr. Speaker, I have talked to General Burns and other people who believe that the safeguards are totally inadequate; they are only safeguards if you trust the word of the people who sign the agreements. Of course, in international affairs we have to trust other countries to some extent,

June 21, 1976
Habitat Conference
but why do we make nuclear reactors capable of being transformed into making plutonium for weapons purposes? Why do we do that with a country like South Korea, which has a militant dictatorship in charge and does not try to conceal its warlike attitude toward North Korea? Only recently in the Argentine we have seen how unstable their regime is, yet we sell reactors to them.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Mac-Eachen) constantly tells us that the safeguards are the best answer. But are they good enough? He has never been able to answer that question or deny that the agreements we have depend on the good faith of the people with whom we make them. He has never been able to defend the fact that some of the people we make agreements with are not to be trusted in this particularly dangerous field although, of course, they may be trusted in other things.
I, therefore, feel that the right of this House to pass a resolution regretting the government's policy in dealing with nuclear reactors is not adequate; there was no leadership in this field and, in fact, the reverse attitude was adopted by government representatives at the Habitat conference in Vancouver.
I just want to mention one other subject, Mr. Speaker, and that is the new international economic order. Once again, we have subscribed to that and have given full lip service to it. But what was wrong with reiterating our concern about it? The minister says we have to let the people of Canada know about it. Why not use the opportunity of such a forum as Habitat to say it once again? It may be repetitive, but we have to keep on repeating the tremendous importance to the world and Canada of making the structural changes that would bring about a new economic order throughout the world. I say that Canada showed lack of leadership when they failed to join with those-which included the NGO and the Barbara Ward group-who urged that there be specific reference to the new economic order. There is none at all.
While we feel that the conference was worth while and that much of great value may emerge from it, we will do our best to urge that action be taken on things like clean water and other matters that were raised. We are duty bound to say to the government that their leadership at that conference was inadequate. That is the purpose of this motion, Mr. Speaker.

speakeroldname: Mr. Maurice Foster (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF GOVERNMENT FOR ITS ALLEGED CYNICAL BEHAVIOUR AT HABITAT CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am happy to have the opportunity to say a few words on this motion put forward by the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Gilbert) concerning the Habitat conference and the resolutions relating to clean water, energy and land use. I had an opportunity to speak at one of the non-governmental organization conferences on nuclear energy, and even though I did not agree with all who attended some of those NGO conferences and their view of nuclear energy, I think it is well that these things are discussed at an international conference of this kind.
I listened very closely to the arguments opposing nuclear energy and I did not find anything very new or exciting in them. I applaud the suggestions that we should have stronger conservation programs. These fit in very well with this government's policy as announced earlier this

year by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie) and in earlier announcements concerning conservation by the former minister. I certainly agree with their aim that over the next few years we should move toward greater use of renewable energy resources.
It is rather interesting that Barbara Ward, who was one of the principal speakers on the panel that I took part in, said in glowing terms that we want to see, 40 or 50 years from now, a greater use of renewable energy. Who does not? We all do. We all know that in the long haul we are going to see very extensive use of renewable resources. That is why the government is investing more in windmill energy, tidal power, solar power, and other renewable forms. But governments today cannot just plan for 40 or 50 years; they have to make plans for this year, next year, the immediate future, the intermediate future, and the long haul. We cannot permit ourselves to say we will spend all our resources for something that is going to be important 40 or 50 years from now. That is why we see nuclear power being very important during the intermediate term, and perhaps the long-term as well, let alone the position that holds right now in our country.
The hon. member for Greenwood suggests that because the government does not agree with some of the positions or resolutions coming from the NGO conference, the government is wrong. Mr. Speaker, international forums of this kind are set up to allow us to discuss these questions. Surely, everyone will not agree with every motion put forward by every individual group.
The motion suggests that Canada places commercial considerations ahead of all others in the sale of nuclear reactors. This is not so. The person who wrote the motion was either cynical about the position Canada has taken over the years or, worse, ignorant of what the federal government has done in fields of safeguards related to nuclear energy. Canada has participated in the International Atomic Energy Agency. We were one of the early signatories, in 1970-71, of the Non-Proliferation Treaty. One of the important parts of that international treaty concerns the sharing of nuclear energy and technology internationally. We have done this; we have provided power plants to various countries. We have done it in the form of providing cobalt beam therepy units for medical purposes, and isotopes for agriculture. Surely, such uses of nuclear technology are an important part of our international trade and assistance to other countries.
Canada has always given safeguards high priority. Indeed, the safeguards which Canada announced in December, 1974, are the toughest in the world. They apply not only to the reactor itself; they apply to uranium fuel used in the reactor, to nuclear technology and to the spent fuel, no matter whether it originated in Canada or elsewhere. The safeguards are to last the full life of the reactor, not just the life of the Np treaty which will run out in less than 25 years. They prohibit experiments which could result in a nuclear explosion of any kind. They provide for fallback inspection, and for monitoring of the use of nuclear energy if the country which is a signatory to the bilateral treaty should abrogate or withdraw from the NPT. Likewise, Canada this year is participating in the discussions and negotiations of the nuclear supplying
June 21, 1976

group, sometimes known as the Club of London. Canada is to encourage that group to adopt international safeguards similar to those Canada has asked of other countries. We are playing an important role in those negotiations.
People who think Canada should get out of the business of supplying nuclear technology and equipment to other countries have not considered how much clout or impact Canada would have with the nuclear-supplying nations if it opted out of sales to other countries of reactors and nuclear technology. It is a question of being on the outside and looking in, rather than of being on the inside and trying to influence other countries to adopt the highest possible safeguards to ensure that our nuclear technology and equipment are used for peaceful purposes.
One of the encouraging ideas at Habitat was that of providing clean water to all peoples of the world. Indeed, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), speaking in the House, indicated that if this were to be a priority of countries receiving our aid, our government would surely co-operate in any way possible. When we are concerned about clean water, we may be talking about water containing chemical and mineral impurities which make its drinking unsafe for health, we may be talking of bacteria in water which will make it unsafe to use, or we may be talking about salt water. As the world's population grows-and it was suggested at Habitat that the world's population will double during the next 30 years-more countries will look to salt water as a source from which to obtain pure water. Many countries are already looking in that direction but many do not possess the oil, coal or other resources needed to produce electricity for desalinating water. Such countries may be thinking of using nuclear energy for desalinating water and for pumping or otherwise transporting that clean, fresh water which is important for human life.
I now shall speak briefly about the CANDU system. It upsets me to note that many in our country who have not studied this system, have not visited Pickering or the new plants at Douglas Point or Bruce, criticize the CANDU system. Most agree that Canadians should not be hewers of wood and drawers of water and that we should advance by becoming an industrialized economy using high technology. Yet such people often criticize the CANDU.
In the world today two basic nuclear systems are in use, the American system, used by many countries, under license from U.S.A. and the CANDU system which produces electricity in our country at rates competitive with those produced from non-nuclear sources of power. It can be equally useful in other countries where it is difficult to produce electricity. I think we should not care lessly criticize this important Canadian technological achievement which enables us to produce energy at low cost. For example, a recent study demonstrated that the Lambton generating station, which is coal-powered, produces electricity at 16 mills per kilowatt hour, whereas the Pickering plant, of roughly comparable size, produces electricity for about eight mills per kilowatt hour.
Further, Pickering uses natural uranium, of which we have a good supply. We have ensured that supplies will last well into the future. The spent fuel does not require reprocessing; to produce electricity economically. In other words, in order for the reactor to be an economically
Habitat Conference
feasible proposition, the spent fuel does not require reprocessing.
The safety advantages of the CANDU have been mentioned many times. Significantly, there has not been one accident anywhere in the world involving commercial, civilian nuclear reactors which has resulted in loss of life.
I want to touch on a couple of other points. The Pickering reactor has operated at 75 per cent efficiency. That compares very well with other reactors around the world. It can be refuelled at full power. It does not require a shutdown. That is one of the reasons it has operated so efficiently. It produced more electricity by January of this year than any other reactor in the world. We should not listen to the glib comments of people criticizing the CANDU system without challenging them.
One of the arguments that was made very effectively in the group with which I participated at the Habitat conference was the efficiency we are now seeing with the Pickering reactor compared to coal reactors. Although there is a large capital cost in setting up nuclear reactors, in a day and age of high inflation the cost of the fuel is a relatively small part of the cost of the electricity produced. If we are going to energy systems which are subject to inflation, the nuclear reactors are relatively less subject to inflation after the initial capital investment. It is rather interesting to note that Pickering B, which is a 2,000 megawatt station identical to the Pickering A station which is now operating, will in fact cost less in constant dollars than the Pickering A station. That is an important point to note in the efficient generation of electricity.
One member opposite, I believe it was the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin), pointed out that nuclear energy is not a good source of energy for many less developed countries. That is very important. I completely agree. The government's review committee which reviews the sale of reactors and uranium always takes this into account. If a less developed country has coal, oil, gas, hydro or other sources which often require less capital-intensive programs, that is a much better system for them. However, some countries do not have any of these indigenous sources of energy. In those cases, nuclear energy may be a suitable system for them. Of course, they need to have an adequate technological base. They need a large enough grid system to accommodate it. No electrical grid should receive more than about 10 per cent of its power from one station. There are these important constraints on nuclear power stations.
Every country cannot use nuclear energy effectively. In spite of this, we have a growing demand in the world for energy. Many countries will be moving to nuclear energy in the future. This is not just because of the situation we have seen in the past, where it was a sort of status symbol to have a nuclear generating plant, but because of the serious shortages of energy, whether from the increased price of oil or a lack of indigenous coal, hydro and other sources. To Canada, these factors are important. Even more important is the fact that the country is willing to submit to safeguards and inspections of the International Automic Energy Agency and is willing to submit to the bilateral safeguards agreement Canada has imposed which go beyond the non-proliferation treaty.

June 21, 1976
Habitat Conference
We see that the generation of electricity is going to increase around the world in future. Canada has been able to cut back its 1974 estimates from some 40,000 megawatts by 1990 to about 25,000 because of the reduction in demand that we foresee.
I wish to spend a moment on the suggestion by the hon. member of the opposition, that there be a moratorium on all nuclear sales to foreign countries. I have already dealt with this in the context that Canada is exerting its influence through the London Club, the nuclear supplier countries, to move toward higher safeguards to ensure that nuclear energy is used for peaceful purposes.
In some ways the non-proliferation treaty was really a bargain between the nuclear weapons countries and the countries which have a nuclear know-how, like Canada, and the non-nuclear weapons countries. The non-nuclear weapons countries said they would forgo acquiring these weapons if the nuclear countries would provide the transfer of technology so that they could generate electricity and take advantage of the use of nuclear energy for peaceful purposes. We will have to ask ourselves if nuclear countries like Canada-

If the countries with advanced nuclear resources say to the countries which do not have nuclear know-how that they are going to cut off the transfer of this technology, are these less developed countries going to keep their side of the bargain of the non-proliferation treaty? In conclusion, Canada has always worked for the peaceful uses of nuclear energy through the IAEA, the non-proliferation treaty, to which we were one of the first signatories, the bilateral safeguards which the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources announced in 1974, and through the work of the nuclear suppliers' club of London to ensure that we have the highest possible safeguards in the world.
Our policy is to support the developing countries with regard to their energy problems, with the use of nuclear energy, provided there are adequate and strong safeguards. It is not to say to them that nuclear power is fine for us, but no good for you. The challenge facing Canada and the world is not to opt out of the problems and difficulties, both domestically and internationally, that nuclear power poses. Rather it is to work with these problems to ensure that it is used for peaceful purposes, and to overcome the tremendous energy problems that face us today and which will face us in the rest of this century.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion proposed by the New Democratic Party affords us an opportunity to step back for a moment and reflect upon Habitat. If the House will forgive me not only do I want to do that but I want also to take a look at some of the other what might be called meetings on specific subjects under the aegis of the United Nations through

the years. I recognize that I do not have very much time and that only in general terms will be I be directing myself to the issues raised. Nevertheless I feel that we in this country, and as a matter of fact the United States too, are entering a period where, unless we are very careful, the public urge government to withdraw altogether from the United Nations or its agencies. I think this would be a very great mistake, and it is in this context that I want to say a word or two about Habitat and the United Nations, an organization that is reaching its thirtieth anniversary.
A wise Canadian, John Holmes, in a speech on December 1, 1975, to the Canadian Club had this to say:
Canada's reputation in the UN is based on a long-standing disposition to avoid dramatic postures, look at critical situations as we find them, accepting the balance of forces as facts of life, and then see that what could be done to move us from a real situation to something better, denouncing the wicked, calling upon legions which do not exist to punish them, or demanding a new United Nations is self-indulgent.
Not only do I admire John Holmes but I certainly believe that what he said is true, that we could indulge in a luxury. I could indulge in a luxury today, if I wished, in castigating the national and international press for its coverage of Habitat. Some people who know more about this than I- therefore most people-tell me that it was easier to get despatches from Bucharest when the world was discussing population, that it was easier to get information from Nairobi when the world was discussing trade, and that it was much easier to get information from Mexico City than it was from the Minister of Justice's (Mr. Basford's) cosmopolitan city of Vancouver. I have no way of judging that, but there are many people in the Department of External Affairs and in government generally who have been quite distressed about the coverage of Habitat on the part of the press of this country.
Of course people were, it seems to me, waiting to pounce on the inevitable. As I understand it, the inevitable came in the last couple of days when an amendment was proposed by, of all people, Cuba, to the principles that many of us hoped could have been unanimously adopted. The Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Danson) is here today and we all heard his eloquent plea that these principles be adopted.
I wonder why it is that we are unable to judge what might be called the humdrum, or that we are unable to get publicity for such basic requirements as clear water, adequate housing, and a better standard of living for people of the world, yet when a mischievous amendment is introduced equating racism with Zionism, the headlines are stark for all to see, and the success of the entire conference, according to some journalists, hinged on whether that malevolent and extraneous part of the whole is acceptable or not to the majority.
I am glad to say that one reviewer in Canada at least, writing in the Montreal Star for Saturday, June 19, Mr. Terence Moore, had this to say:
It is important not to judge the United Nations Habitat conference simply on the basis of what it said about occupied lands and aggression and resettlement of refugees. Those are subjects of intense legitimate interest and friends and supporters of Israel are naturally upset by the conference's implied condemnation of Israel.
But it has been clear since last November where the great majority of Third World governments stood on Middle East politics.
June 21, 1976

The headline writers should not have been surprised at that intervention at Habitat. We should really judge other parts, and I hope that the motion introduced by my hon. friends of the New Democratic Party will allow us to focus as well upon the positive aspects not only of Habitat but of the United Nations in general.
A journalist said to me even today, "How does Habitat affect your constituency or your province of New Brunswick?" I suppose that after a while in this House one gets used to xenophobia of that kind, and had I more time to reflect I might have been able to give this journalist friend of mine a catalogue of potential lumber orders that could have been processed in the province of New Brunswick, interesting new techniques in building and so on, which obviously the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce would want to promote around the world. Many of these techniques have their origin in the province of New Brunswick and in my constituency.
Must we always measure things, Mr. Speaker? Surely we must not. I pose the question and then answer it. Surely we cannot pose questions having only to do with what is a functional problem of housing and water, or such functional problems as food supply as were posed in Rome, or of pollution in Stockholm, or population in Bucharest, or of how women are treated in contemporary society in Mexico City. In some of these conferences there were political interventions, but this should not surprise the member of parliament. It should not surprise anybody who is an advocate of the United Nations and who realizes how essential is the United Nations to the future of mankind.
I once read what was said, I was going to say by a distinguished Archbishop but I suppose that archbishops do not need any such adjectives so let me just say by the Archbishop of London and leave it at that; others can judge of his distinction. In a sermon or homily he asked that immigration be taken out of politics. As a practising politician I resent, with great respect to the reverend gentleman, the concept that such things can be taken out of politics or public life. This is the place of politics, and I think that is right. It will be of no surprise to anybody that the UN is a place of politics. It so happens that many recent conferences have dealt with the functional problems faced by men at the time of their movement, and I profoundly hope upward movement, toward a better life.
I think it is good news that the New Democrats of Canada have taken the government to task on various parts of Habitat. I prefer not to do that, but not because of any feeling of bon ami toward the government. God forbid that ever happening to me, although I suppose it might in a weaker moment just before Christmas. Otherwise I am prepared to take the government to task on any occasion.
What I am really trying to say is that we should not worry that the world is engaged in the political process. We should not worry that the New Democratic Party has seen fit to try to dissect some problems faced by Canada and the world. After all, this was only the host country at Habitat.
My belief in this aspect is that we must be careful not to become so obsessed with political issues and manifestations of them, amendments to resolutions and so on, that
Habitat Conference
we lose the concept or the real purpose of the United Nations, which is to harmonize-and this is part of the charter-the national interests of the states which belong to the United Nations.
I get increasingly worried about people who would like to step back from the UN and throw it up because they happen to be in opposition to the majority, or even equate the majority with some form of tyranny. I think this is hyperbole that does great damage to the UN as an institution, and also that it is terribly self-serving. Many states, if they have any historical perception at all, could presumably turnabout and suggest that for many years there was a majority in the interests of those states, that are now part of the majority, that was equally as tyrannical. That is a terribly complicated sentence, and I realized that as I got it half out. What I am really trying to ask is, is a majority any more tyrannical because it occurs in 1976 than one which occurred in 1953, 1954 or 1955? Was the majority of the veto, that excluded for a whole generation a quarter of the world's population, a tyrannical majority? I think not.
Canada is in a very interesting position because next year, if present indications go as expected, we will be once again a member of the Security Council, and we will have the opportunity to work very carefully and, as some wise observer of the scene informed the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin), the hon. member for Saint-Michel (Miss Begin), and myself the other day, the Secretry of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen) will have to have a good hotline down to Port Hawkesbury when Canada sees what becomes of members of the Security Council. Officials of the department will need instructions instantaneously, and perhaps the Secretary of State for External Affairs will have a hotline in his aircraft when he shuttles back and forth to his beautiful riding.

speechtext:
The hon. member for Saint-Michel talks about a gas station, if I heard her correctly. That might be one way, of course, of publicizing the United Nations and Canada's interest in it. It might be one way to inform Canadians of the implications for all of us of the responsibilities that will be on the government and on the parliament of this country when we become a member again of the Security Council, because the gas station, or wherever it is the Secretary of State for External Affairs gets his telephone calls from Ottawa, will be the point of information for the public in that community. This is the dilemma the Minister of State for Urban Affairs has faced too, because there are not enough people in gas stations who understand the aspirations of this country vis-a-vis the United Nations. This is a communications problem that the government wrestles with in its domestic affairs as well.
In any event, when we become a member of the Security Council we will have to do two or three things, and I should like to list them. We will require a much more clear identification of our policy priorities as a nation. We will require more active diplomatic pressure to implement these priorities, and we will have to be considerably more frank than we have been. I am not now gainsaying what the Minister of Justice and the Minister of State for Urban Affairs said at Habitat. I was not there. I must say, how-

June 21, 1976
Habitat Conference
ever, that the Minister of Justice has a very highly developed press section which grinds out material. Our mail boxes are full of it, and I think this is a delightful innovation in the Department of Justice.
We also will require more selective participation in United Nations debates and activities. The voting provisions, yes or no, on major issues according to our assessment seems to me to be an absolutely fundamental essential. It would be a peculiar Canadian experience, just as the patriation of our constitution would be the final sort of identification of our nationhood, if we stopped looking all the time to see what other nations did, and took the initiative on votes because we are peculiarly Canadian. I have no doubt that we are mature enough as a country to be able to do this. I do not say this in any boastful way, but today this is a positive thing for the United Nations.
Then lastly, and I guess I mentioned this in the Port Hawkesbury part of my speech, we will have to focus on improving opinion in Canada and our understanding of our opinion of the United Nations.
I suppose this is an intervention, afforded me because of the initiative of the NDP on this opposition day, which allows me to say that it is a good, plus thing that once again we are going to take up responsibility of Security Council membership. This will mean not only general support for the United Nations, but also that this is a government priority and that there can no longer be any question about that. I am sad to say that this is the case with some other countries, that is, selective withdrawal from the United Nations and its agencies.
I do not want to get in over my head on issues, but I think it is a sad sight to watch members of the United Nations trying to withdraw selectively from the ILO, for instance. Certainly the United States interests have been deeply troubled, but it does not do the United States foreign policy very much good, if I may say so candidly, for them to threaten to get out, take their marbles and go home, and not pay their dues if such a course of action should not occur. It is obvious that I would not at all favour the total giving up, but I think that is an option that could be exercised. We could give up altogether and decide that large conferences, international as they may be, with long and boring speeches and with the relentless pressure that will be on this country when we become part of the Security Council, are not in the interest of Canada. I would hope, despite the criticism by the New Democratic Party, that no one in this parliament would seriously consider that it is in the interest of Canada to withdraw altogether.
The United Nations, as the Charter says, has as its purpose the harmonizing of the interests of nations. It is difficult for parliament to harmonize the interests of this country; God knows it is a relentless preoccupation of all of us to try to harmonize the interests within our country. Therefore I fail to see why anyone would be surprised if the harmonizing of interests beyond the borders of this country should be equally relentless and equally demanding. I am glad to say I have no doubt that Canada will not want to withdraw. We will see that in the area of air law, sea law, housing and water-

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF GOVERNMENT FOR ITS ALLEGED CYNICAL BEHAVIOUR AT HABITAT CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when I read again the motion of the opposition which was moved by the New Democratic Party member for Broadview (Mr. Gilbert), I just cannot understand what is the common denominator which inspired this motion, if not a general and fundamental attack, valid or not, against the assistance policy of the government of Canada.
As a matter of fact, why relate the conference on human settlements called Habitat in Vancouver and the sale of CANDU reactors? Why talk about the so-called cynical behaviour of the government and in addition about our supposedly conflicting and bold statements on the subject of clean water?
I frankly cannot understand why criticisms are levelled against the federal assistance program. To begin with, if I quote a short excerpt from the speech made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in Vancouver on May 31 for the opening of Habitat, it is because in my opinion he clearly states the intention of Canada. He said:
The globalization process is speeding up and already a new world is developing. The world-wide responsibilities which our wealth leads us to assume constantly remind us of the fact. No country can remain aloof and conscious of what it has nor keep its possessions secret. Pressures from numbers and needs compel all of them to become more open with others and share more widely the secret of their resources. Failure to account is becoming impossible. Willingly or reluctantly, we are at the beginning of a new era of universal control.
I am quoting in the House from that speech because perhaps very few Canadians and parliamentarians read it and unfortunately could not attend the Habitat Conference since we are constantly sitting here instead of being in our constituencies.
To my mind, the Prime Minister was thus stating quite clearly that Canada intends to help. At the time, the opposition said, and today I speak of the New Democratic Party, as well as all the other parties for that matter: Why good intentions? Again, we are getting empty words: where is the money? Where are the concrete proposals? I heard, to my astonishment, the hon. member for Edmonton-Strath-cona (Mr. Roche) introduce the idea of the Nairobi common fund, the fourth UNCTAD conference in the debate. In fact, from the numerous interventions, I gather there is a general attack against Canada's foreign aid policy. I shall come back to the common fund later on.
June 21, 1976

So, to my mind, the intent is clear. So, where is the money, were is the concrete help? Here, Mr. Speaker, I should like to recall what Habitat is. I am not an expert, but I am very much interested in the matter. Habitat was one conference among several United Nations manifestations. It is one conference in time, not a permanent organization, nor an institution that operates full-time.
It is one conference which attempted to give the people an awareness of one of the most acute problems of our times, a problem that is completely unknown in Canada, unless one has gone from southern Canada and some distance into the north of our provinces or the Territories. Those places are, to my mind, a source of shame to all Canadians. I am thinking here of some of the communities inhabited by the first settlers of our country, in which none of us would want to live, and of which we are ashamed. In other words, Habitat was meant to make Canadians aware of their wealth.
It was a forum in which resolutions developed and not a forum of commercial negotiations. It was a forum of the resolutions crystallizing everybody's goodwill to develop material forms for the promotion of the places where human beings must live, to determine how and with which basic elements they have to be able to survive. Many resolutions have been established, several of which are only recommendations because they are directed to national sovereignties, the others being commitments, at least moral commitments, because they are directed to the international community.
I did not understand the remarks of the hon. member for Fundy-Royal (Mr. Fairweather) who was unable to translate into reality . . . Mr. Speaker, may I call it six o'clock? I would like to ask permission to continue at eight o'clock.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF GOVERNMENT FOR ITS ALLEGED CYNICAL BEHAVIOUR AT HABITAT CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at six o'clock, when we adjourned the debate, I was saying how surprised I was that the hon. member for Fundy-Royal (Mr. Fairweather) had apparently failed to translate into reality what the conference on human settlements in Vancouver could bring to Canadians and I just described that kind of conference which is only a momentary event and not a permanent organization. Its goal is to make people like Canadians who live in a very wealthy country aware of the most crucial problems faced by three quarters of the world- lack of housing, lack of basic sanitary facilities in houses or cities and mainly lack of clean water with all the endemic diseases it creates.
Apart from that awareness development aspect, the Habitat conference gave us a large number of resolutions which were not submitted in advance and negotiable, according to the wishes of the international community to which we all subscribed. Three of them could be easily
Habitat Conference
identified and I think important to mention them in the face of serious accusations such as those made in the socialist party motion.
The first concerns us very much as it relates to the audio-visual library received by one of our universities in Vancouver. My colleague, the parliamentary secretary for urban affairs, the hon. member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier) has already mentioned it. The two others concerned us but particularly the Canadian assistance and I mention it because I am deeply disappointed by the character of that motion which condemns the whole foreign assistance policy of Canada concerning the Third World. I shall resume them rapidly and I quote the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen) who, on June 1 in Vancouver, said bluntly and I quote:
First, Canada is prepared to provide, through bilateral Assistance and cooperation programs, favourable answers to assistance proposals in the field of human settlements that will be submitted by its partners in those programs.
He goes on:
In addition, we will use our influence within multilateral development agencies to encourage the latter to prove favourable as well.
I conclude with a second and last quotation of his text:
Second, we consider as particularly worthy the proposal to establish regional training centres aimed at those having to plan and direct human settlements. For several years Canada has been giving its support to the Asian Institute of Technology located in Bangkok and to its program of human settlements. We think this program deserves continuous support and, in this way, might serve as a pattern for similar programs in other regions.
Finally, as a concrete recommendation, I will mention the one in which Canada had proposed that countries of the planet would all have access to drinking water by 1986. The final recommendation, as I understand it, was much more moderate than the emergency position advocated by Canada. There was agreement so that that goal might be reached by 1990, that is within 14 years. That shows fairly well the extent of the problem.
Coming back to the money issue, there can be no reference to cynicism since we already committed $210 million over the next three years on the last resolution alone. I therefore wonder whether opposition members are ready in the context of budgetary restraint, we had to impose on ourselves and every Canadian to fight domestic inflation which is the cause of specific ills-particularly in the area of employment-whether they are ready to fight in support of the suggestion that the external aid budget, now approximating $1 billion but still 5.2 per cent only of our GNP while it should be around 7 per cent, if they are ready to fight to maintain that in real terms and or increase the amount of money extended by Canada to the third world.
I wonder what kind of arithmetic the socialist opposition is following. But when we commit ourselves to increase n-fold, to give urgent priority to water purification projects to ensure drinking water to all communities in the world, mainly through our bilateral programs maybe through certain international bodies but mainly through bilateral agreements. The sums of money voted by Parliament are limited, they are already committed formally or through pre-agreements in the case of certain projects. Therefore, who is going to pay, where shall the money come from for that indisputable priority, drinking water for every human community on this planet?

June 21, 1976
Habitat Conference
Apparently, it is all very easy when in opposition to level that kind of criticism, but without coming to a single view. When time comes to vote subsidies, suddenly we hear all kinds of subtle criticism, suggesting we throw the money away on military aid which is totally inaccurate. Today we are faced with the horror of a South Africa where officially more than one hundred dead were registered, not even taking the trouble to tell before the world what is happening to 80 per cent of its citizens, who are treated as a minority in a totally shameful way.
Confronted with the deep contradictions regularly apparent among the opposition as to the suggested importance of the help effort, which is in my view an indisputable priority, and the subsidies Parliament has to vote regularly, I feel this is a very serious scandal. The New Democratic Party added in its opposition motion that we are putting our commercial interests above everything in Canada's nuclear sales. Such statement is really gratuitous and stupid. Canada-and I shall not emphasize that point-may not be the best seller since everyone knows that, being committed towards some countries, it is now dealing with foreign economies whose inflation rates exceed 200 per cent and that despite this fact, in the so-called conventional contracts, Canada is obviously not first of all a seller. First and foremost, although it was a seller, Canada is a member of the non proliferation treaty. It was one of the very first members, as soon as the treaty was put into force in 1970. At this time, about 100 countries only approved this treaty. At the same time I can say: 100 countries only and 100 countries, already, because that is a lot. By the way, I regret that some advanced countries in the nuclear field, such as France and China, have not accepted to sign the treaty. I can also say that this treaty has been greatly strengthened in 1975 when it was signed by five EURATOM member-countries, Belgium, Holland, Luxemburg, the German Federal Republic and Italy, and by countries such as the Korean Republic and many others which are not yet so-called nuclear states.
Why did we sign the non-proliferation treaty? Why did we systematically study this treaty? Why did we judge two years ago that it was not severe enough as far as standards for countries are concerned? Why did we take initiatives from which we heard through the London Club? We took all these measures because we are convinced that we must, according to the treaty and according to the principle of human solidarity, share, for pacific aims only, a technology which is often the only energy source which can be used in human settlements. That is why I often think of the spectacular example which is often given, that of the electricity for the town of Karachi in Pakistan. We could also find other examples. So, this is often the only energy source which can be used in human settlements and we have no right to judge that our stability, our democracy and our sufficiency are superior and to refuse to others what we judge as good for ourselves.
I shall end with a few remarks on the accusation that Canada's trading interests come before the other interests of humanity when it comes to selling nuclear reactors, and I shall underline that from now on Canada's policy, as far as its public bilateral development assistance is concerned, will be to refuse Canadian nuclear reactor to countries which are not members of the non-proliferation treaty. Mr. Speaker, before I end-I see that my time is coming to an

end-let me refer to an accusation made during this debate by the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Roche), who said that we were not involved in development assistance to the Third World, giving as an example our so-called absence or negativism towards the common fund in Nairobi, during the month of May.
The UNCTAD worked during the whole month of May, following the Manilla declaration of the group of 77, to stabilize, among other things, the basic commodities market in the world. Not only did we endorse the principle of the common fund, but we did actively participate in it. It is evident however that it was a bit utopian to try to delude the developing countries by having them believe that we thought that this was the best and only solution. Politically, we accepted the fund because it had become the very symbol, if I may say so, of the international new economic order. I see that my time has expired-

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF GOVERNMENT FOR ITS ALLEGED CYNICAL BEHAVIOUR AT HABITAT CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am obliged to our colleagues in the New Democratic Party for bringing forward this motion. Frankly I am confused by some of that wording, and to this moment that confusion has not been particularly alleviated by the speakers from that party.
I wish to assure the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Danson) that I am not one of those who wish to judge the success or failure of Habitat. I do not think that is our responsibility or, still less the responsibility of those who attended the conference and who were subjected to the
June 21, 1976

pressures, and emotions, and effort required to make a reasonable input into such a conference. My only experience which is comparable was a food conference in Rome some time ago. Since that time I have felt that I, least of all, am able to judge the success or failure of such a meeting. I think we should leave that to the future. It is much too early for a final verdict on what took place in Vancouver.
What concerned me very much was the attack, which had some validity, on Canada's credibility which arose from that conference. That is not the same thing as judging a conference in terms of success or failure. It would seem to me that people can say to Canadians with some justification that those who live in glass houses should not be the first to throw stones, or they may say to us, "Physician heal thyself", or we may say to them, "Do as I say and not as I do".
A very good example is the water issue. It is very difficult for me to understand how Canada can retain its credibility in terms of pure, clean, acceptable water, as a preacher of this position, when we have reports daily of the sins we have committed in terms of our own water resources.
I was very impressed with what the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Roche) said, and I believe I can quote him fairly accurately. It was to the effect that developed nations do not follow up their rhetoric with action. I am not particularly happy to be branded a hypocrite, Mr. Speaker. It would not bother the parliamentary secretary, I am sure. She has already intervened without waiting to hear what I have to say, which is fairly consistent with the conduct of members of the government in this regard.
I was not particularly impressed with the fact that our Minister of the Environment (Mr. Marchand)-and I rise particularly because the motion deals with environmental matters-says that our action and interaction with neighbours throughout the world will depend on the government's ability to judge its action or interaction by the votes it may get in the next election. As the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona said, that gained wide press coverage. I think that is unfortunate, though I do not object to them saying that in an election campaign. I think it is part of the fight in an election campaign.
The Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Danson) says he did not say that. I asked the minister that very question in this House in the unavoidable absence of this minister, and he did not deny for one moment that it is what he said. I gave him every fair opportunity, and despite the intervention now of the Minister of State for Urban Affairs, the Minister of the Environment did not deny that statement. I gave him every opportunity to do so. I do not think it brought any credit to our Minister of State for Urban Affairs-and I join my colleagues in congratulating him on his contribution; I was very proud of him, but I was not proud of his colleague when he made that particular reference which was so widely quoted in the Canadian and international press. I was embarrassed as a Canadian to read that our contribution would be dictated by an election result that was some time away. Despite the intervention of the Minister of State for Urban
Habitat Conference
Affairs, I think the low water mark was that reference by the Minister of the Environment.
The motion deals with the commercial criteria with regard to nuclear power, and I should like to deal with that matter as it affects the environment. I think we are going to be judged on our actions by the developing countries. I am afraid of being accused of hypocrisy, and I think one of the things we are going to be judged on is nuclear power and nuclear waste.
The most serious environmental impact of nuclear power in my judgment is in the field of the management of waste produced by reactors. This waste is composed of radio-actinides which have extremely long half-lives-in the case of plutonium 25,000 years. This means that a given quantity of plutonium will be half as radioactive in 25,000 years as it is today. At this rate it would take 250,000 years for a moderate sized quantity of plutonium to become safe.
There are a number of methods of disposing of the waste. We have investigated burying it in salt, and we have investigated burying it in stable geological formations-[DOT] and even shooting it into the sun. At the moment Atomic Energy of Canada seems to be leaning toward the geological disposal of waste in the pre-Cambrian shield.
Aside from the obvious problems associated with even geological disposal of the waste, it is important to remember that, as of today, no waste has ever been disposed of successfully. In the United States liquid waste is stored in steel tanks which, although built to very high tolerances and with double walls, have been known to leak. Substantial leakage of waste could obviously pollute the water table of a considerable area leading perhaps to the closure of an entire community. In addition, waste in temporary storage is vulnerable to theft, which given its toxic nature could have grave security implications.
Another hazard of nuclear power as far as the environment is concerned-and here again we are going to be judged on the way we deal with our environment-is that caused by thermal pollution created by nuclear power plants. Because of the high steam temperatures at which the facilities operate, vast quantities of cooling water are needed-about 50 per cent more than the conventional plant; thus, given present technology, nuclear power stations need to be located near very substantial bodies of water.
All of these considerations may be deemed theoretical, and perhaps they were until the Port Hope incident. They are not theoretical any more but are very, very real. Human error in the past was translated into significant dangers to children who were not even born when the mistakes were made. Therefore I think, and I urge upon my colleagues, that if we are going to be dealing with the less developed countries that the environmental considerations be given a priority and consideration far beyond that given by the government to date.
The economics of nuclear power are increasingly coming into question. In the last three years capital costs, inflation, and the general cost of capital have made nuclear power decreasingly economic even though oil prices have quadrupled during that period. At present trends, oil-fired power stations will be competitive with nuclear stations in the very near future. In fact the Barber report commis-

June 21, 1976
Habitat Conference
sioned for the energy research and development administration in the United States calculates that at about $30 a ton for power station coal, nuclear stations under 600 megawatts are uneconomic. Ontario Hydro estimates that this is about its average cost of coal delivered to its power stations.
Another economic problem of nuclear power as far as less developed countries are concerned is that the current vendors of nuclear stations sell only 600 megawatt or larger units. In a less developed country with a relatively unsophisticated power grid, a 600 megawatt unit represents a tremendous proportion of the total electricity requirements. This can mean that the less developed countries in question will develop an excessive dependance on one power source. In light of the fact that most power stations only operate between 50 and 70 per cent of the time, this leads to immense distortions in the power supply.

speechtext: Who wrote that?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF GOVERNMENT FOR ITS ALLEGED CYNICAL BEHAVIOUR AT HABITAT CONFERENCE
speechtext:
The parliamentary secretary shakes his head. Can he tell me where a developed country can purchase a nuclear power station under 600 megawatts on the market place today? It is impossible. A country which purchases a unit that size or greater becomes tremendously dependent on that one single unit. In terms of safety it is probably the biggest issue confronting the advocates of nuclear power. This is a most controversial question, technically, and I claim no expertise.
I suggest that claims for the over-all safety of nuclear power plants are usually based on United States experience. They are summarized in documents such as the Rasmusian report, which suggests that the probability of a fatality from a nuclear accident is extremely small. Apparently the chance of being killed in a nuclear power accident is about as great as that of being killed by a meteorite. Because laymen do not usually readily understand probability theory, and because these statistics may easily be distorted, there is widespread unease about the safety of nuclear power in communities located near nuclear power plants.
Another problem concerns the use of nuclear material by terrorists. Quite apart from the potential which exists for making bombs from plutonium, a potential which is very likely not as great as has been commonly stated, it must be borne in mind that plutonium is a highly toxic element.
