speechtext: Will the hon. member please address the Chair?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF GOVERNMENT FOR ITS ALLEGED CYNICAL BEHAVIOUR AT HABITAT CONFERENCE
speechtext:
I do not know if the hon. member wishes to participate in the debate. I listened to him not long ago and could not understand one thing he said. He made a most inconsequential contribution. Perhaps we are getting even. The hon. member may not be prepared to understand; I do not know.
One pound of plutonium can kill many times over every man, woman, and child on this planet. This worry is magnified by the exponential growth of world plutonium stocks. By 1980 200 tons will have been produced; the figure by 1985 will rise to over 700 tons.
My second point relates to the wording of the motion. The motion refers to "the government's bold statements on such environmental matters as clean water and its inability or unwillingness to enforce minimal standards in Canada, as in the case of the Syncrude plant in northern Alberta." The mover of the motion referred to the Great Canadian Oil Sands plant, instead of the Syncrude plant. I would have been happier if the motion had referred to the Great Lakes as an example, particularly as the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Gilbert), the mover of the motion, is more familiar with the Great Lakes than with the Athabasca oil sands. I think the example in the motion is most unhappy. However, since the motion mentions the Syncrude plant, my remarks will relate to Syncrude as well.
I accuse the Minister of the Environment for creating a confused situation with regard to environmental matters on which other countries will inevitably judge us. For example, what is the minimal standard if we use the GCOS yardstick? Is it to be 287 long tons per stream day, which is apparently the standard being set for Syncrude? Or is it 40 long tons, a standard which many allege can be reached if sulphur scrubbing equipment is installed in the plant? Further, what is the cost of such equipment? On the one hand we have reports saying it costs $60 million; in other cases companies allege that the cost will be up to $1 billion. Is the equipment any good? On the one hand some people allege that, for a $60 million expenditure, emissions can be reduced to 40 long tons a day. On the other hand some companies say that the equipment is unproven, unsatisfactory, and will never meet that particular target. The Minister of the Environment ought to answer such questions; so far he has not done so.
Who has authority for dealing with such environmental matters? The Minister of the Environment says that certainly the federal government has no authority. Despite the legislative authority of the Clean Air Act and the Environmental Contaminants Act, the minister has said repeatedly in this House and elsewhere that this is simply a provincial matter. Although the federal government is largely involved with the Syncrude operation, the Minister of the Environment has said repeatedly in this House that the federal government has no responsibility with regard to environmental matters. If this is true-and I am speaking theoretically only because I do not agree that it is- why in heaven's name has the minister not agreed with his provincial counterparts on what the acceptable level ought to be?
Surely developing countries will judge us for our inadequacies, since we cannot determine who has authority and, even if there is joint responsibility, what the commonly acceptable standard ought to be. Really, that is the thrust of the motion. We tell developing countries how concerned we are about the environment; we brag of our environmental assessment studies. And in fact we have commissioned environmental assessment studies. One was


June 21, 1976
undertaken with regard to Syncrude. But we do not do what we say we will do.
The Environment Canada comments on Syncrude's environmental impact assessment were so extensive as to merit a further study which is now under way, financed 50-50 by the federal and Alberta provincial governments, and will cost around $40 million to complete. The study is to be completed in 1985 owing to the comprehensive scope of its investigations. Syncrude, however, will begin operations in 1978, which leaves a hiatus of seven years. The spending of $40 million of taxpayer's money will result in a study which we shall receive seven years after the start-up of plant operations. And we say to developing countries, do as we say, not as we do. We tell them how concerned we are about our environment; yet we shall not complete a major environmental impact study until seven years after the Syncrude plant is in operation.
Apparently the NDP are concerned about the Athabasca tar sands. I do not wish to enlarge on what the hon. member for Athabasca (Mr. Yewchuk) said, but I am concerned about the example to which the motion we are debating alludes. In Alberta the main thrust of the forces opposing Syncrude has been managed by Mr. Grant Notley, the sole NDP member of the legislative assembly. Mr. Notley reportedly has a highly qualified staff of three working for him full time, on a generous research budget provided to him as leader and sole member of one of the opposition parties in the legislature. On occasion Mr. Not-ley's researches have steered him up some blind alleys. For example, Mr. Notley claimed that the GCOS emissions were killing thousands of water fowl in the Athabasca area. The hon. member for Athabasca this afternoon, as have others at other times, completely rejected such claim as being inaccurate. It is unfortunate that the mover of the main motion did not use a better example to illustrate concern for the environment.
I come back to the Minister of State for Urban Affairs and say that I will not judge him on these matters. He and the government will be judged on these matters by others some time in the future. On the other hand, I join my colleague from Edmonton-Strathcona in complimenting the minister on his speech at Habitat. I say to him, sincerely, that I thought the Minister of the Environment made a most unhappy intervention at that conference. Second, so long as we are hypocritical about environmental matters in Canada, it will be difficult to show developing nations the leadership they expect of us in this field.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF GOVERNMENT FOR ITS ALLEGED CYNICAL BEHAVIOUR AT HABITAT CONFERENCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, at the outset of my remarks may I congratulate the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Danson) for acting as chairman at the Habitat conference and for performing his duties under conditions which, as many know, were most trying.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF GOVERNMENT FOR ITS ALLEGED CYNICAL BEHAVIOUR AT HABITAT CONFERENCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF GOVERNMENT FOR ITS ALLEGED CYNICAL BEHAVIOUR AT HABITAT CONFERENCE
speechtext:
The motion the House is debating refers to the cynical attitude the government adopted at the Habitat conference on the question of pollution and the provision of clean water, as well as to what has happened pollution-wise in the Alberta tar sands development. The last point relates to the way this country has sold nuclear reactors to
Habitat Conference
various countries of the world with the attendant pollution and safety problems.
In the debate at Habitat and again today, the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Roche) brought in the whole question of the Habitat conference as it relates to the whole new economic order and the discussions that had taken place in Nairobi. He mentioned that the Vancouver conference was a successor to several important U.N. conferences held in the past few years, notably the food crisis conference in Rome, the population crisis conference in Bucharest, the rights of women conference in Mexico City, and the environmental conference in Stockholm.
There is an old Biblical saying that is familiar to most people: There is faith, hope, and charity, but the greatest of these is charity. The line that I am going to take tonight is that there is food, clothing, and shelter, and the most important and greatest of these is food, even though I realize that the Habitat conference was supposed to be primarily directed to the problems of human settlement. In reality a great deal of the time was spent trying to allay the political by-play or inter-play between the mid-East forces that unfortunately crept into that conference, as it has into so many UN conferences in recent years. Perhaps it was unavoidable.
I listened to the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona and part of the speech in reply by the Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Miss Begin) who would very well have been talking about the new economic order in the same way as the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona. I realize that since the world food conference in Rome we have not moved as quickly as possible. Obviously if we are going to get into a new economic order it involves what was discussed at Nairobi, including commodity agreements, raw materials, preferential tariff agreements between the developed and underveloped world, changing trade patterns, a host of structural changes that need to take place in the underdeveloped world as well as in the developed world in order to bring about a greater redistribution of resources as between the poorer and richer nations. We all know that in the long run that has to be done. A start has to be made.
There is something, though, about which I am becoming increasingly concerned. My fears have not been allayed since the conference in Rome. I refer to the fact that we underplay too much the necessity of foreign aid in the traditional sense.
I was particularly struck by this fact last night in watching the CTV program "W5". There was a discussion by two people, one of whom was Dr. McTaggart-Cowan, a well known Canadian scientist who did a study of the oil spill disaster in Chedabucto Bay. The other was Dr. Schneider, I think his name was, a climatologist from one of the midwestern states. They predicted that we have fed into the computers too much of these historical climatic cycles without any reasonable room for random variations that can completely change the picture with regard to food supplies in the short run as it affects our country and, therefore, millions and millions of people in the underdeveloped world.

June 21, 1976
Habitat Conference
Since the world food conference in Rome, books and articles have been produced with regard to the question of the lifeboat theory, the idea that wealthy countries should help only the most promising of the poorer countries. I asked the Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs a question with regard to the comparison of the GNP. The answer she gave me is correct; it is much less that 1 per cent. She did not state, and I am subject to correction on this, that the close to $1 billion figure she quoted includes $100 million to $150 million for military expenditures in these countries. I do not consider that conducive to helping these countries to obtain food or better human settlement.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF GOVERNMENT FOR ITS ALLEGED CYNICAL BEHAVIOUR AT HABITAT CONFERENCE
speechtext: That should be million.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF GOVERNMENT FOR ITS ALLEGED CYNICAL BEHAVIOUR AT HABITAT CONFERENCE
speechtext:
I should have said $250 million, I think it is. Anyway, I am subject to correction. It may be $150 million. My point is that the distinction needs to be made between military expenditures as a part of the foreign aid program and the real foreign aid program relating to food, shelter, and things like that.
As I was saying, the lifeboat theory is still prevalent. There has been much written about it, probably as a consequence of the world food conference in Rome. The idea is that the wealthy countries should help only the most promising of the poorer countries, since spreading resources too thin could jeopardize chances for survival of the strong as well as the weak. There is the suggestion that wealthy nations should make distinctions between poorer nations in the spirit of "triage", the first world war medical practice of dividing the wounded into survival categories in order to concentrate medical resources on those who could truly benefit from them, and to ignore those who would die even with treatment or survive even without it. Some proponents of these theories cite projections from the Club of Rome's statistical model "The Limits to Growth" to add a seal of technological legitimacy to their modern-day malthusianism.
These apolyptic concepts are provocative, and the threads of truth they contain do have frightening implications. Moreover, momentum for this pessimism has been building, abetted by full page advertisements in major newspapers, articles in important international publications, and a marked increase in the demand for triage speakers on American campuses and television panels.
As a recent copy of the New York Times magazine noted, the campaign has had its impact. Many leaders who have been in the forefront of efforts to help the needy are currently mired in an uncharacteristic mood of inertia. And the lifeboat and triage theories offer a rationale for their passivity.
Yet a close look reveals that the theories are not appropriate to today's realities and need not be for tomorrow's. In fact reasonable and hard headed assessments of available figures suggest that it is well within the power of humanity to produce enough food to prevent masses from starving. The fact that it is possible to refute the current lifeboat and triage theories, however, as Barbara Ward notes, does not mean there is no food crisis. Various food crises and inadequate distribution systems have affected nutritionally the status of millions of children from low income families, and unless dramatic policy decisions are

taken soon this trend, I am afraid, is likely to accelerate over the next decade, with ominous consequences. That in face is the reason why the lifeboat and triage theories must be refuted now.
I was happy to see that in a recent interview Mr. Hopper, Canada's head of the International Development Research Centre, had this to say about the triage concept. He said it is an unworthy concept. It assumes that there is nothing you can do, or that the resources that it is going to take to do it are just so colossal that you cannot afford to expend them. He says that this is a perfectly valid classification in the heat of battle on the battlefield. If I may quote him from an interview in the Globe and Mail for November 3, 1975, he says:
But when it comes to the world food situation, "I don't think we're at anything like that limited capacity at the present time. I don't think we're out of time and I don't think we're out of resources."
He went on to point out that some nations that would be left to their fates are in fact agriculturally very productive-India, for example. He says that the concern should be not to abandon them but to transform their traditional agricultural practices into scientifically based ones that will increase their output of food.
I want to go further than that, Mr. Speaker. I think it is most important to recognize that the basic concept of squeezing the world into a single lifeboat is wrong. The aim should be to build more lifeboats. You then increase food production in needy countries in the longer run, while in the shorter run you supply them with the needed food, so that the many possible and in some cases probable famines that will be facing the world will be readily dealt with.
The view of helpless countries holding out begging bowls for a few kernels of grain is I know the last thing in the minds of all development agencies and low income nations. We all know that in many countries there is nothing politically more difficult to handle and more damaging to a nation's pride than food aid. However, realities are realities, and it does not do to have leaders such as, with all due respect to his memory, the late emperor Haile Selassie who, as we now know, tried to hide the fact of some famine in Ethiopia. Pride can only go so far.
Based on today's technologies, we know the opportunities for major growth in food production are there. Scientific breakthroughs are possible. Some research projects are already approaching fruition and others offer interesting promise. In any event, if we take the lifeboat and triage theories to their conclusion and deny aid to many hungry nations, what ultimately will happen to them? This is the reason we have to get up to the one per cent of GNP that the Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs mentioned is her dream. It must not be a dream, even in a period of national restraint; it must become a reality in one of the most relatively affluent countries of the world, even though our growth rate over the last few years, in GNP-per capita terms, has gone from second among the nations of the western world to sixth or seventh.
Furthermore, evidence is beginning to accumulate showing that great efforts are being made now at reducing
June 21, 1976

population growth and improving nutrition. These two factors are linked together far more closely than once thought. In many poor areas the best way to lower the birth rate is to provide a family's children with a decent chance for survival by the economic transformation of their society, as well as the provision of food aid in the short run. If half of their children die before reaching their productive years, parents will feel that they have to conceive a great many children-common belief puts the figure at eight-to ensure two surviving sons. So ironically the rate of population growth could be lowered partly by providing food to keep children alive and healthy.
It is hard for Canadians to realize, Mr. Speaker, as became clear at the Habitat conference, what it is like to be in the shoes of those who have to live on $200 a year. It is evident across the country, despite the attempts of officials to break that barrier down, that it is pretty tough for us who are used to restaurants with plenty of food, who are used to three square meals a day and a pretty good roof over our heads, to realize the suffering endured by these people.
If we try to imagine what it is like for a family to live on $200 a year, Mr. Speaker, first of all let us take out the furniture, except for a few old blankets, a kitchen table and one chair, take away the pantry, save for a few potatoes, dismantle the bathroom, take away the house and move the family to the toolshed, and take away all the other houses and set up in their place a shantytown.
My House leader has reminded me, Mr. Speaker, that I do not have much time left, so some of the things I was going to say will have to be left unsaid. I hope on another occasion I will have an opportunity to make some further points. Let me conclude by congratulating the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Gilbert) on pointing out today that one of the great problems in our country in regard to housing is land speculation. Although we have developed this question before in the House, I wish he had developed it a little more today in relation to the food policy of this country and foreign food aid. Some of our best agricultural land is owned by these greedy speculators, and the provincial and federal governments are allowing them to go ahead as in the fertile Niagara Peninsula.
Let me remind us all of what John Maynard Keynes said after the first world war when he predicted what was going to happen in Germany. I suggest we remember this today. He said:
Men will not always die quietly. For starvation, which brings to some lethargy and a helpless despair, drives other temperaments to the nervous instability of hysteria.
We are seeing that at the present time.
These in their distress may overturn the remnants of organization, and submerge civilization itself in their attempts to satisfy desperately the overwhelming needs of the individual. This is the danger against which all our resources and courage and idealism must now co-operate.

speakerposition: Minister of State for Urban Affairs
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF GOVERNMENT FOR ITS ALLEGED CYNICAL BEHAVIOUR AT HABITAT CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to have this opportunity to engage in this debate and I thank the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Gilbert) for introducing it. It gives us the opportunity to talk about matters which I think are very important and which we do not discuss all that often, even though there have been accusations of cynicism. I
Habitat Conference
think we can make them both ways, though it would not be very productive.
The important thing to remember is that we had a fine delegation at Habitat, one that was truly representative. It was not only a federal delegation; it was a national delegation and included all levels of government, non-government organizations, our native people, and women, of whom I wish there were more on the delegation, who acquitted themselves admirably under the outstanding leadership of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) who led the Canadian delegation. I think they did us credit, and I include all the members of the Canadian Habitat Secretariat. I think they did us credit; the people of Canada, the Habitat Secretariat, and Commissioner General Mr. MacNeill did us credit. The arrangements, as all the delegates and all the United Nations people said time and time again, were second to none. Perhaps more important was the fact that the hospitality of the people of Vancouver was second to none. The warmth, the spirit, and the interest was noticed everywhere the delegates went, and this situation was repeated time and time again.
I certainly want to thank those who have paid tribute to the role I played there. It was one of considerable interest.
I must say, however, that the conference did not solve the problems of the new international economic order. It could not deal with those things which the UNCTAD conference at Nairobi did not really resolve. There is still trouble in Ireland, and there is still tragedy in Lebanon. The Middle East problems have not been solved. The United Nations Habitat conference on human settlements was not able to solve those problems which neither the General Assembly nor the Security Council have been able to resolve so far. Many people ask: well, is that not a tragedy? That is not what the conference was about. These are the things that most of the people directed their attention to day after day in tough sessions. This is what the people directed themselves to in the long period of time in preparation for the Stockholm conference.
These people dealt with settlements. They reached conclusions on many of the human settlements issues. Perhaps 90 per cent or 95 per cent of the substance for which the conference was called was agreed upon by consensus. As the Minister of Justice has said, it was not such that we could vote or approve the Declaration of Principles by consensus.
We should not lose sight of the real progress that was made and for which the conference was called. There were no surprises. We were not surprised when issues which some consider extraneous or irrelevant arose. Delegates in most cases were not briefed on them. They did not have instructions from their governments on them. The conference was not really competent to deal with them, but these reflected the real world, and also something else which we Canadians had the opportunity of learning. It reflected that these things which we sometimes consider extraneous and irrelevant are very central to other people. I think that is the lesson we must learn.
There were over 140 nation states represented, plus many observer groups, liberation groups, and non-government organizations. We were getting the full spectrum of

June 21, 1976
Habitat Conference
the world and it has shifted, just as the United Nations has shifted. The conference is suffering from that democratic fault of having the majority have its way, and this was reflected very much there.
If we look back, as we will, and as we are beginning to do now at the Stockholm conference on the environment, we will remember these things. Very few people, except perhaps a few UN watchers or specialists, will remember the difficulties at the Stockholm conference with the recognition of the Chinese delegation, or of the German Democratic Republic delegation not being represented. I forget the details myself. When we look back and forget all the turmoil of the so-called extraneous political matters we remember the substance of what the Stockholm conference was all about. Many things have happened as a result of that. There are very few nations in the world without environmental programs, and at that time there were very few with such programs or even with environmental ministries. The word "ecology" was perhaps known to a few academics, specialists, and scientists, but now it is used by school children, and felt with their hearts.
There are many programs now on the environment under the auspices of the United Nations Environmental Program in Nairobi, for instance, the one begun following the conference regarding depollution of the Baltic Sea. Even the preparatory arrangements leading up to the conference have resulted in progress. Canada and the United States signed the Great Lakes Water Quality Agreement as the Great Lakes Water Quality Agreement as a direct result of the interest created in preparing for such a conference because it focused attention on this. Very few people know about the Barcelona agreement for the gradual depollution of the Mediterranean Sea which was signed a few months ago. It involves the nations around the Mediterranean, including those opponents in the Middle East conflict. Even they reached agreement on this fundamental issue which was of human and social concern. This is the way we will look back at the United Nations Habitat Conference on Human Settlements in Vancouver.
I am told there are some 20 territorial disputes going on in the world today. I am sure that in another 20 years there will still be 20 territorial disputes going on. They probably will be different ones, but the work started at Habitat and in the preparatory process will continue, and its impact will continue to be felt. That is what is important and that is what made Habitat worth while.
I have mentioned consensus. We must remember that there were three committees, including Committee Two which dealt with policies, strategies, planning, institutions and management. It brought in a report under Mr. Ansari of Iran which was a consensus report. Committee No. 3 under Mr. Aria of Venezuela dealt with shelter, infrastructure and services, land, and with public participation, and it brought in a report by consensus. The conference dealt with water quality.
It was Canada which led the fight for water targets. It was said here today that we made no financial commitment. No nation there made a commitment for funding in respect of water quality, but we fought for targets in order that there would be piped pottable water to every community by 1990. Canada would have preferred the 1986 date, but perhaps we are a little too progressive and there was a

consensus reached in respect of 1990. For Canada this is important because we forget sometimes that in our own communities we do not have clean, piped water, but we hope to in all Canadian communities by the 1980's.
We are prepared to make commitments through our external programs. This is not cynicism. It would have been the height of cynicism or self-righteousness for us to tell the developing nations what their targets should be, because there were also programs of national action. This was a critical part of the whole Habitat Conference which was made up of sovereign states which must set their own targets, their own goals, and their own priorities. If their priorities reflect that which was reflected by the conference, that is, a high priority on water, Canada is very much ready to respond.
Certainly it took the magic of Barbara Ward to dramatize this for the whole world, but that consistently throughout was Canada's position. In addition, the University of British Columbia, as was mentioned, will be the scene for the unique and innovative audio-visual program which will be for the transfer of information. Not only the audio-visual program itself, but all the other documents and upgrading and enriching it as time goes on, will be of advantage to Canadians and also to other people throughout the world.
There were plans for international co-operation and institutional arrangements, and this came of Committee One under Father Muhoho of Kenya. It is true that a consensus was not reached on a statement of principles, but it is rather striking that but for perhaps ten or 15 words there would have been a consensus. It was with sadness that I noted this was all that prevented us from reaching a total consensus.
It is this planning for international action which should go to the setting of priorities and the preparation of programs to which Canada will respond as we do already through our CIDA people. In this way we exchange internationally technology, know-how, and resources. Many things are still to come as a result of the conference.
The level of consciousness throughout the world was raised immeasurably in this whole area of human settlements. Country after country had programs which were going on before Habitat. Some made them a national effort. Through the activities of many, many people in the forum under Mr. Van Puttan of The Hague, and perhaps fortunately with the help of people like Barbara Ward, Margaret Mead, Buckminster Fuller and Mother Theresa, there was a consciousness that permeated every facet of Habitat, and those people who were interested became fully aware of what the basic problems are in the world, where our priorities and commitments should lie. So it was hardly a waste.
Many steps forward were taken. We did not solve the problem of human settlements, I might say also. We just started the process. This was the second stage of a process. There was a long preparatory process. Habitat was the time when we made our commitments, and now is the time of implementation. There will be a time of monitoring too. There will be monitoring at a national level which we will do here in Canada, I hope in the fall when there will be
June 21, 1976

meetings involving our delegation and the non-governmental organizations, and there will be international monitoring through the United Nations both on a global and on a regional basis.
In so far as our own concerns about human settlements are concerned we face some issues very squarely. There is the question of land which really reflected the Canadian reality. It exposed us. That is fair enough because it was a national delegation. I must say I take exception to the reference to particular names. The name was raised of Mr. Teron, the secretary to the ministry. He really fought very hard for a very liberal position in those committees.
There were others present there who represented Canadian reality, the mixed economy and the federal nature of our country. That I consider a great assist because now it has exposed the problems for Canadians to see, for governments to see. I now am making contact with the ministers responsible in the various provinces across the country so that we can face that problem squarely together for the very first time.
There are jurisdictional problems, and there have been problems presented before. However, there has been a reluctance to sit down together to do something about it. I do not care if we sit down together or work in parallel, if the municipalities sit with the provinces or if we all sit together, or whether or not the private sector is there, the fact is that it has to be approached with urgency because obviously the problem is there and it will not go away. We have come to realize that certainly land is not a commodity but is a resource. This is the way in which we have to face it. Regrettably the debate today and elsewhere focused on the windfall profits in land, which are a problem. We have ways to deal with them through taxation. The provincial governments have ways to deal with this matter through taxation, and I guess also the municipalities.
We have to examine the matter much more thoroughly. However, that is only one element in the high cost of land and housing. There are many other factors. It is an important element, but it is not the most important. We have to sit down and look at it in the totality. Our job is not just to recapture profits for the community, which we do in many of our programs now; we also have to reduce the problems in respect of serviced land so that we can get housing at a lower price.
We have made our commitments in respect of water. We have to work very hard to meet them. We are making progress through our municipal infrastructure programs, and even this morning we had further meetings on how we could move into the area of remote communities where the greatest problems are.
There is the whole question of energy conservation, the design of our communities, and the need for proper urban transportation. This problem certainly has developed, and is one to which we certainly will have to give much greater priority as a result of this conference. This is something to which we are addressing ourselves now.
Then there were the problems of the Third World. We have problems in Canada. All developed nations have problems, or perhaps the industrialized nations, because some of those less industrialized are perhaps more developed as societies. But we can hope. We have the resources
Habitat Conference
and the skills, and all we need are the political will and the priority to make them work. But in the Third World they do not have that luxury. When you are dealing with the squatter settlements of Asia, Africa, Latin America, and even in some North American areas to some extent, we see problems of immense proportions.
We talk about children and families living in refugee camps in Palestine and elsewhere. In this regard we have immense problems to which we must address ourselves as a world community. When we look at the villages in Asia, Africa, and Latin America which have never known clean water, where the women perhaps spend five hours a day hauling water, never really clean water, when the same water is used for cooking, drinking, washing, laundry and for defecating, end where virtually 100 per cent of the people suffer from water-borne disease, our problems fade into insignificance.
I do not believe our answer is to be able to provide housing for all the people of the world. If we can get that one first priority of clean water in each community then we have made immense progress. Then we need some decent sewage disposal, health services, and education, and then people will start building their own homes and their own communities. Then they can have a piece of land which they can call their own. Then they can have tenure of land, some pride and some stake in the community. Then things will happen. Then the problem of population, and not until then, will start to fade because then, as one of the hon. members opposite said, the families who have eight children, two of whom survive, will realize that maybe if they have two or three the two or three will live, and they will have the education and the will to do the proper family planning.
Those are the things which also come home to us as Canadians and as members of a world community. Organizations like CIDA and others have now focused in on the problems of water, sewage, and of human settlements, as has the World Bank and as have other international institutions. We must really face these issues squarely. We must realize that Habitat was not to cure all the problems of the world. It made immense progress in those areas it was intended to address.
I believe I have responded to many of the questions raised by the hon. member for Broadview, or certainly my colleagues have in the area of nuclear waste and in the area of the environment. I did want to deal particularly as I have with the question of land where the incremental gain being recaptured is only one element in the whole land picture, as I am sure he realizes quite well. I am sure that because it was a federal delegation, and because the provincial ministers were present, there was a disposition to meet on this subject. There is no commitment, but I will be in touch with my provincial colleagues to address this issue together as quickly as we possibly can.
The hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Roche) indicated that the Minister of .Justice, the leader of the Canadian delegation, reserved Canada's position on these important issues. I think he will agree in all fairness that he made it perfectly clear that there was a lot of area for compromise and for agreement and consensus. There was only one area which prevented us and all other nations from supporting it, and that indeed was unfortunate.
14722

June 21, 1976
Habitat Conference
Other members have zeroed in on other points of concern. I note that the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) mentioned the question of rhetoric as opposed to action. Of course none of us can afford this kind of selfrighteousness. Conferences are made up of words, and politicians use words. So do non-governmental organizations which sometimes do not have the responsibility for implementation, so I do not think this is a case of the kettle calling the pot black. It is a matter of realizing our responsibility in this respect and making commitments, as nations did.
The hon. member for Fundy-Royal (Mr. Fairweather) of course mentioned the question of press attention. This was raised. It was rather a disappointement because I am told by UN hands and by the press people generally that the press arrangements were the finest ever made for such a conference. Yet editors thought it best simply to focus on those highly contentious issues which were not central to the conference, those about which it is easier to write perhaps, and which attract more attention.
Having said that, I think the Vancouver press and the British Columbia press generally were very responsible and covered the conference in great depth, as did radio and television. Many journalists took a serious interest in the whole issue of human settlements and reported it very well and in depth. Indeed I am rather pleased to see the press reaction now, a week or so later, which did not take an interest in the conference before but in doing an assessment now is doing it wisely.
The hon. member for Perth-Wilmot (Mr. Jarvis) spoke about the danger of self-righteousness. The hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond (Mr. Hogan) was cynical about our commitments with regard to water. I think that a healthy degree of cynicism is good, but so is a healthy degree of naivete. I would not like to be out of balance either way.
The hon. member for Fundy-Royal spoke about politicization. I should like to repeat that this was not surprising. We hoped it would not happen, but this is the real world and it did happen. As a matter of fact it might be unproductive because the Third World is not monolithic, and because sometimes it detracts from the substance of these conferences, and more and more people are coming to realize that it is best to keep the specialized conferences as much to the point as possible.
We cannot believe for a moment that other problems will go away or that they are indeed extraneous. They are not extraneous to us as a world community, they are problems with which we must deal very seriously because if we forget the little children in the Methari Valley in Kenya, the children in the refugee camps in Palestine, or those children who have not survived the Warsaw ghetto, then indeed as a world community we are in great difficulty. I ask hon. members to assess this conference properly, to see what happened at Habitat, to look at the accomplishments, the plusses, and to hope for more of them in the future, but also to see what the alternatives are so that nations can get together and air their problems.
Even if we do not like the real world, we must be exposed to it. It is much better to have those differences on

the table with the cards face up so that we can deal with them rationally and reach solutions. We in Canada cannot isolate ourselves from the world and its problems, and this was another benefit of Habitat because it brought them home more closely to us, more closely to the people of British Columbia and especially of Vancouver who really had a close-up view of the entire conference.
I respect the cynicism of the hon. member for Broadview, but I do not share it. I think that we accomplished a great deal at Habitat, and I think the world made a great step forward there. We will look back, not in 20 years but in two or three years, and see major action taking place as the result of this conference, as we have seen major action taking place as the result of the conference on the environment at Stockholm.
As I said, Habitat reflected the reality and the despair of the world, but also the hope and the highest ideals of mankind. I appreciate the fact that having a big heart and good-will is not enough-there must be commitment, there must be action to follow. But I am proud of Canada's role as host of Habitat and as a delegation at Habitat. I think all facets of the Canadian presence contributed well and did Canada proud.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I should like to ask the minister a question, if you will allow it. Can the minister tell us what specific plans he has for a follow up to Habitat. He just touched lightly in his address on the subject. The non-government organizations which attended Habitat are most anxious to have follow up meetings across the country, and I wonder if the minister would tell us now what plans he has to promote the national program of action which came out of Habitat in a series of seminars on a regional basis across the country, perhaps culminating in a national meeting in the winter of 1977.

speakerposition: Minister of State for Urban Affairs
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF GOVERNMENT FOR ITS ALLEGED CYNICAL BEHAVIOUR AT HABITAT CONFERENCE
speechtext:
It is not only the non-government organizations but the non-organized governments that must get together now. I think we must leave sufficient room for assessment so that non-government organizations will be encouraged, as they are being encouraged, to meet, assess and monitor us, politicians. I do not want to give specific dates but I hope that not too late in the fall there can be a national meeting of non-government organizations. We have to decide if that is not too early, if perhaps we should not allow a longer time range to give more time for assessment. Certainly action in this direction has been started. I do not expect miracle answers overnight, but the process has to start quickly and we need the co-operation of the provinces and municipalities, which I am sure will be happy to participate.
In so far as external programs are concerned, I am aware of the fact that CIDA is looking at these new programs to respond to them. I think we will look at our energy conservation programs, and urban transport will get greater priority, all of this within the context of what are real economic restraints. I think this puts a different complexion on them, but I believe that this follow up and monitoring must start very quickly even on an international plane. The secretary general will be reporting to EcoSoc in Geneva this August, and then he and I will be reporting to the General Assembly in New York in the fall. We hope we can reach agreement on the institutional arrangements so
June 21, 1976

that international action can start. The UBC project is now under way and going to work immediately so that the very valuable information which was collected from many countries will not be dissipated immediately after the conference.
I can assure the hon. member that we will not let grass grow under our feet. This will not be fast enough to satisfy him or me, but we will certainly try as best we can.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in view of the fact that only 30 minutes are left in the debate I have no way of forcing my preference over other members who want to speak,, but what I have to say will only take seven minutes in order to allow equal time to the remaining four speakers who want to speak.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF GOVERNMENT FOR ITS ALLEGED CYNICAL BEHAVIOUR AT HABITAT CONFERENCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF GOVERNMENT FOR ITS ALLEGED CYNICAL BEHAVIOUR AT HABITAT CONFERENCE
speechtext:
I agree with the minister. I find that I myself am not guilty enough of ethnocentricity. I find that I am not guilty of measuring the standards and values of other nations based on the values I hold in this country to be right, good and equal for Canadians. I think that if more of us were guilty of ethnocentricity in reverse, we would perhaps be a little more concerned about some of the conditions we discussed, that were discussed at Habitat, and that were mentioned by the minister tonight.
Even though there are problems abroad, that does not in any way wipe out the real problems facing Canadians with respect to housing. There are people in this country who have a great hope, and they hope that one day they will be in a position to be able to own their own homes. That hope exists among young people in spite of the failures of the minister and the government. These are the days when old men dream dreams of how things used to be, and young men have visions of despair. Why has this hope turned to despair? Why are young people having to give up the right or the possibility of owning their own homes?
Just in passing, I was disappointed with the answer the minister gave me this afternoon in the question period. I was disappointed that he did not level with me and this House with reference to the one year mortgages which are a rip off to first time home owners in this country. The minister chose to evade the question.
I hope that there is still time for repentance, that the minister will read his answer, come to his senses, and tomorrow with tears streaming down his face stand in his place and right the wrong, and tell the people of this country what he intends to do with reference to the situation which has arisen with the bait and switch of one year mortgages.
In the time left to me I would like to bring to the attention of the minister the situation in the United States where, primarily in the area of housing, they make use of tax incentives, housing credit assistance, and cash subsidies, with the emphasis on tax incentives. I am wondering if the minister has given consideration to this and whether he would give thought to moving in this direction and providing tax incentives on interest paid on mortages- perhaps over 8 per cent or 9 per cent, but that could be decided upon-and perhaps to avoid double taxation, tax
Habitat Conference
credits for taxes paid on municipal property to be deducted from revenue, primarily personal income tax.
I think that the advantages of this would be numerous. It would ease the burden of interest rate fluctuation, particularly high interest rates, on the taxpayer in a visible fashion; stimulate demand for home ownership; assist new families purchasing homes by allowing higher interest costs to be deducted from the generally lower incomes of younger families in the early years of family formation; and assist in building long range stability within the housing field. This scheme avoids tax upon tax, which I have already mentioned, and which has been part of past schemes. Home ownership ought to become a reality.
Just 50 years ago in this country education was considered to be a privilege, and now we consider that to be a basic right. I want to say categorically that I believe it is a basic right of expectation of every Canadian to own his own home or to have the option to own his own home. However, the option to own one's own home applies only in a certain context. We want to come to grips with that. It is not good enough, day after day, to give us the kind of verbiage that the minister gives us so well. It is not good enough to articulate the problems and then wring your hands in despair and say it is not possible.
Sir, Canadians from one end of this country to the other cannot understand why it is, with our vast resources in land and natural resources and with our hundreds of thousands of acres of land and timber, that our economic system does not allow people to own their own homes. It is not good enough that we cannot put our interest rates in order and that you, sir, cannot put your House in order to bring this about.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to join the debate on Habitat, 1976, which I believe was the largest United Nations conference ever held. It is certainly a credit to the UN, to the great city of Vancouver, to the Government of Canada and its delegation, and especially to the Minister of State for' Urban Affairs (Mr. Danson) for his devoted leadership.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF GOVERNMENT FOR ITS ALLEGED CYNICAL BEHAVIOUR AT HABITAT CONFERENCE

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF GOVERNMENT FOR ITS ALLEGED CYNICAL BEHAVIOUR AT HABITAT CONFERENCE
speechtext:
As we have heard, some praise Habitat for its results and some criticize, but I believe that the most important thing about it is that it happened. I do not think any reasonable person can deny that a new initiative had to be taken on such a high priority subject as human settlements. Human settlements, of course, mean much more than housing. They mean such things as land and space, water and disposal, a stable climate and an agreeable environment.
95570-31)4

June 21, 1976
Habitat Conference
I also congratulate my friend, the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Gilbert), for raising this subject, although I am afraid I cannot agree with his skepticism about it.
I would like to speak for a little while about one particular subject, as did the hon. member for Algoma (Mr. Foster), who is also the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, and that is the subject of Canadian policy with regard to nuclear sales. Human settlements depend not just on structures and resources, but also to a very large extent on that basic commodity, energy. There is no question that, as a result of the recent changes in the world energy situation, many countries must turn to sources other than oil to meet their increased requirements. It is the obligation of the world community, including Canada, to help them to do so. There are a number of sources which must be adequately explored and developed, including indigenous energy resources such as coal and hydro, which in many cases were not considered at all seriously in the days of cheap oil. That has only come about recently.
New technologies, also largely ignored until recently, will have to be examined urgently and carefully. Nuclear energy, especially nuclear fission, however, is the major technological option available today. It is by no means applicable in all cases because of the scale of power requirements and power grids, and because of the massive investments in capital required. Nuclear technology is highly complex and sensitive, and only a relatively small number of countries have the technological resources to manage it adequately.
The government recognizes these limitations in deciding on export sales. It is, however, the responsibility of Canada as a member of the international community to make energy resources available to other countries, and in those cases where nuclear energy is the most appropriate, to share that technology.
Such sales, however, are only authorized under the most stringent international safeguards against the diversion of Canadian assistance to non peaceful uses. Canada is prepared to forgo sales where these guarantees are not available, and is acting vigorously in all international forums to raise the world standard of guarantees to levels which give the greatest protection against diversion to explosive use.
In general, Canadian export sales decisions are not, as charged by the opposition, based on an overriding commercial motivation. The government welcomes Canada gaining national benefits through world acceptance of CANDU, but this is not the central element in reaching decisions on nuclear exports. Nuclear transfers are motivated by the responsibility to help with the world energy situation on a number of fronts, including, but by no means restricted to, nuclear. Sales are made only on the basis that the facilities Canada supplies are built to the best and safest standard and are operated with the best protection for the environment. They are only authorized when there is a high degree of assurance that the facilities will be used for agreed and purely peaceful uses. Having said that in generality, there are a number of questions posed recently on the specifics of this particular subject. I should like to quote a few of those questions, and some of the answers which are widely appreciated.

I can think of about ten different questions that arise: the diversion of spent fuel; the return of spent fuel to Canada; Canadian nuclear export policy in general; the non-proliferation treaty as a pre-condition of sale; justification of Canada's reactor sales to non-NPT countries; a moratorium on nuclear exports; CANDU licensing safeguards; bilateral inspections on nuclear safeguards; CANDU licensing negotiations, with Italy in particular; safeguards in uranium sales, and finally, environmental considerations.
We should look at one or two of those questions, Mr. Speaker. First is the question about diversion of spent fuel or misuse of spent fuel. It has been alleged that the CANDU reactor is particularly suited for the purpose of diversion if a country desired to do so. Regardless of verification techniques, how can the government be supporting the sale of such a potential bomb maker to countries like Argentina and the Republic of Korea? The answer is that both Argentina and the Republic of Korea have a nuclear power plant from other sources. Canada is not supplying reprocessing equipment and technology. All nuclear reactors produce plutonium and there is no essential difference in this respect between CANDU and light water reactors exported by other suppliers.
The quantities of spent fuel available in Argentina and the Republic of Korea will be considerable, quite independent of the CANDU reactor to be constructed in these countries. The CANDU facilities will be under stringent safeguards, including a Canadian veto on reprocessing. This may hopefully lead to an upgrading of safeguards on reactors sold by other suppliers.
Let us look at another question. Why is it that Canada does not insist on what appears to be the ultimate measure of safeguards in terms of restricting the use of plutonium by the Republic of Korea by having all the spent fuel from the reactor returned to Canada? The answer is that this option was carefully considered by Canada and it has been decided, as we have noted in the House previously, that on balance such a requirement would not be the best to serve the interests of Canada.
Apart from the serious environmental problems that such a course would create, it would not prevent a country, intent on violating an agreement, from retaining the fuel either by directly abrogating the agreement or by noncompliance. In the event of abrogation of the agreement, that country would be left with a significant stock of spent fuel stored for cooling which is essential before shipment, as well as fuel in the reactor and fuel about to be inserted in the reactor. Since this quantity of material would be more than ample for any immediate production of plutonium, the margin of protection against diversion would not be nearly as significant as the question indicates, at best it would mean a reduction in available stocks over a very few months.
Canada does have the clear right to prohibit reprocessing of fuel from the reactor and has given clear notice that it is not willing at this time to agree to it being carried out. In the government's view this stipulation, together with the inspection mechanisms in place, provide an adequate level of protection against diversion.
June 21, 1976

Perhaps I should raise one final question, the third out of those ten, and that is on the general Canadian nuclear export policy. The following question has been posed: in light of the criticism by such a well-informed critic as Ralph Nader that nuclear exports to Third World countries are an example of "criminal responsibility", how can the government continue to maintain that it is pursuing moral objectives in selling CANDU reactors to Third World countries? In particular, how does the government respond to criticism that less developed countries do not have the technological capability to manage such complex technology safely?
The answer is we believe that in speaking in the very extensive debate in this House on March 23, we outlined the government's policy very clearly. The government does not maintain that nuclear power is, in all cases and at all times, the only or even the most desirable energy alternative for all developing countries. It is recognized that likely only some Third World countries at any particular time need or are fully able to operate such a sophisticated energy source. What we are saying is that in the cases where the need and the ability exist, this energy should not be denied.
The moral problem is a complex one and should be examined in all its dimensions. I cannot accept the suggestion that Canada should fail to observe its international obligations to help developing nations achieve economic progress. Surely the way to meet the concerns raised is not to cut off access to nuclear technology but to provide the means and techniques to ensure its use, with safety, and under safeguards.
I might note in this connection that Canada's approach in marketing the CANDU system is to ensure that the reactors are not only built to Canada's high standards, but are handed over to operators of high technical competence and run under international safeguards earlier outlined in this House.
The other seven questions can certainly be answered with an equal amount of thoughtfulness.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I should like to say that the world must continue to address itself to all basic human and social concerns such as settlements and all means to that end, no matter how challenging those means may be. A fortunate people, like Canadians especially, cannot afford to shirk that responsibility.
Some approaches, such as nuclear energy, will themselves give rise to new concerns and new questions such as the questions which I have just reviewed. We are answering today's questions and we must answer tomorrow's, but answer them we will.
Canada is in the forefront of such progress of benefit to all mankind. A great deal of the credit for this goes to our federal government and especially to our Minister of State for Urban Affairs. I for one shall be pleased to continue supporting him and all the efforts of our government both at home and abroad to take care of the needs of people. Habitat was an important step toward that goal.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF GOVERNMENT FOR ITS ALLEGED CYNICAL BEHAVIOUR AT HABITAT CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the brief time that I have to devote to the subject of debate tonight there are some areas I should like to discuss, though possibly not in the context of the motion.
Habitat Conference
I should like to start with the question of a pure water policy and the environmental concerns that were expressed. While I have some very serious reservations about the Habitat conference they really do not lie upon the shoulders of the government for I honestly believe that the minister set out in a very forthright fashion to produce something that nations around the world could be proud of, and set out to do a job that the United Nations and Canadians would be proud of. I think he was frustrated in that.
Some of the Third World countries set political priorities; that was the way they viewed it, and in my view it was unfortunate. The minister made reference to a developing situation at the United Nations some years ago which concerned the German Republic and China, but those are not the countries that are creating problems today at the United Nations; instead it is the countries that need our help. In my view those countries are going to have to be dragged through the doorway to that help, and they are going to resist every inch of the way. They used Habitat as a political forum, and I think that unquestionably they are the ones which are going to suffer rather than the countries devoted to human settlements.
Having said that, Mr. Speaker, I should like to move to the question of pure water. This is an area of great concern, and perhaps the classic example of this concern is demonstrated by the series of questions I placed on the order paper in 1974. On December 11, 1974, I placed on the order paper the following question:
What is the estimated tonnage for the next five years of human waste that will be dumped from vessels plying the Great Lakes?
The Department of the Environment replied:
The estimated quantity of human sewage, including the usual 32 gallons flush water per person per day, is 7 million tons for the next five years.
I put the question on the order paper because the then minister of the environment had indicated that, in her view, it was not necessary to take action with regard to the amount of human sewage being dumped in the Great Lakes from Great Lakes vessels. She felt that the five-year moratorium provision was fine.
My second question of that date reads as follows:
What is the estimated average cost per commercial vessel for the installation of holding tanks for human waste?
The department's response reads as follows:
The estimated average cost per commercial vessel for the installation of holding tanks for human waste ranges between $23,000 for new tugs to $74,000 for new lakers and between $28,000 for existing tugs to $81,500 for existing lakers.
If the federal government had wanted to clear up a serious difficulty, it could have provided subsidies. For smaller vessels the subsidy, amortized over five years, would work out at between $5,000 and $10,000, an insignificant sum to pay for something which would help to clean up the Great Lakes. I use the word insignificant because, in terms of total pollution of the Great Lakes, the quantity of human sewage dumped from vessels is relatively insignificant.

June 21, 1976
Habitat Conference
The third part of my order paper question reads:
What improvements for the holding or disposal of human waste in Great Lakes ships are anticipated in five years time and at what cost?
In 1974 the then minister had said she was not prepared to do anything for five years. In part, the answer of the department informed me that in five years time I could anticipate:
... Construction of approximately 12 shore-based reception facilities, strategically located, and designed to receive commercial ships' sewage for subsequent discharge in a manner which ensures adequate treatment. The anticipated total cost of these facilities... is $2,500,000 assuming that, existing wharf space will be made available at no charge.
I wonder how far $2.5 million would go, even if paid as a partial subsidy, toward the installation of sewage holding tanks in Great Lakes steamers.
Lastly, I asked in my order paper question:
To what estimated percentage degree does the dumping of human waste from such vessels contribute to the pollution of the Great Lakes?
According to the department's answer, approximately .3 per cent is attributable to ships' crews.
When you consider that .3 per cent of pollution is attribuable to ships' crews, but that in five years Great Lakes ships discharge seven million tons altogether into the Great Lakes, it is clear that the total volume of human sewage dumped into the Great Lakes in five years is in the order two and one third billion tons. That is shocking.
The minister indicated that we have a clean water policy. Let me say that the people of Kootenay West are most interested in that policy. I hope the Department of Regional Economic Expansion will agree with British Columbia to provide in the valley a pipeline to carry pure, potable water for all communities along the Columbia River or, assist the province and municipalities concerned by providing for pumping stations to pump water from the Columbia River into holding areas where the water can be purified for human consumption and industrial and agricultural uses. At present the area cannot expect to develop unless it has available considerable additional volumes of clean water.
The water is available. Unfortunately in the Columbia River below the High Arrow Dam one sees the pollution effects of a pulp mill and also of a lead smelter. Would that not be an excellent program for DREE? What an excellent contribution the department would make to providing the pure water advocated by the government. The government could help us in two areas; one is in my riding; the other is the Great Lakes.
I am concerned about the question of nuclear reactors. I suggest that anyone wishing to debate that subject will open up a can of worms on my side of the House. We have heard many statements on the subject from the government benches. Perhaps the most flowery and inconsequential statements are made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen). There is beautiful rhetoric, adding up to nothing, except pending disaster. In my view CANDU sales are an example of fiscal irresponsibility. The government is ignoring its responsibility in the nuclear field to all countries of the world. Expert after expert has offered testimony showing that CANDU is a financial calamity, a nuclear catastrophe and should not be

considered. I contend that if the government were concerned more about pure water and less about heavy water, it would have accomplished a great deal more.
We have seen the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Danson) beating his breast and expressing concern because people in the poorer countries of the world must drink lousy water. Heaven knows, I have seen it myself and could not agree more. I suggest it is time the government wound down its CANDU policy and wound up its pure water policy.
I now come to the tar sands. I am greatly concerned because Alberta has claimed sole responsibility for eviron-mental controls with respect to the tar sands. I saw the same attitude displayed two years ago in British Columbia. I saw evidence of pollution connected with a DREE project in my riding. When I wrote to the provincial government, asking what they were prepared to do, they said, in so many words, "You are a federal member; keep your nose out of this." I say that since federal funds are used in DREE projects of that kind, the province's attitude was irresponsible. I could say much more; unfortunately I see my time has expired. May I call it ten o'clock?

subtopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS-LOCKOUT OF AIR CANADA FINANCE BRANCH EMPLOYEES-POSSIBLE RESUMPTION OF MEDIATION
LABOUR CONDITIONS-LOCKOUT OF AIR CANADA FINANCE BRANCH EMPLOYEES-POSSIBLE RESUMPTION OF MEDIATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for the last three or four weeks I have been calling on the government to direct the Auditor General to conduct a complete audit into the financial fiasco, or complete financial breakdown, of the Air Canada finance branch in Winnipeg. I was hoping, after what happened last week, that the minister would take action. Unfortunately the government had sluffed me off and referred the entire matter to the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications. In no way can the committee conduct an audit into the financial fiasco at the finance branch of Air Canada in Winnipeg. Nevertheless, I shall welcome seeing Air Canada representatives appear before the standing committee as I wish to discuss several matters with them, and will be glad to hear their comments.
May I allude to a statement made to the Winnipeg Free Press on June 17 by Michael H. Cochrane, vice president of the Air Canada finance branch. He denied union allegations that mismanagement had contributed to the airline's record $12.5 million deficit last year. He said two major audits by private firms in the last year had thoroughly studied Air Canada accounting procedures and found them satisfactory. That statement is completely false. There was no detailed accounting whatsoever by any accounting firm in the finance branch.
He went on to say that the audits were conducted by Clarkson and Gordon Ltd. for the Estey inquiry into the airline last year, and by Coopers and Lybrand for the airline itself for 1975. The deficit, he said, was caused by a major decline in passenger traffic, rising fuel bills and other escalating prices.
In the Coopers and Lybrand report in the 1975 financial statement of Air Canada they state:
Our examination included a general review of the accounting procedures-
The general review did not consist of a detailed study into the airline billing at the finance branch, Winnipeg.
Also, under the terms of reference from the Estey report, Clarkson and Gordon were required primarily to review the Winnipeg centralized payment system, the Montreal payment system, the Dorval purchasing system, certain local branch purchases and the system of authorization for expenditure. The review did not include payrolls and did not examine, except in a very summary fashion, the subroutines related to specific disbursements.
As a result of this review Clarkson, Gordon & Co. prepared a description of the disbursement systems and submitted this description to the commission, a brief summary of which is included in Chapter 5 of the Estey report. They did not go into detailed billing whatsoever.
I discussed this with the employees of the finance branch in Winnipeg. They told me that no outside auditors came into the finance branch to do a detailed study. Some employees recalled outside auditors dropping by in 1972. However, there have been no outside auditors doing any review since 1972.
Adjournment Debate
Also in the Estey report it is recognized that, under the Financial Administration Act, the Auditor General is eligible to be appointed as auditor or joint auditor of the corporation, but such has not been the case in the past. It is certainly time that it was done, especially in view of the charges by the CALEA union in Winnipeg. Also, in the Estey report it states, and I quote:
There is no doubt that the final fiscal responsibility for Air Canada resides in Parliament when all other resources fail and therefore Parliament is entitled to the fullest and clearest financial reporting.
That is all I ask for, a clear, precise report from the Auditor General. The government has a responsibility to send the Auditor General there in light of the serious charges by the CALEA union in Winnipeg.
I have cited many cases of mismanagement over the past two weeks. One was that there are no longer any enforced controls for travel agents reporting ticket sales. As of October, 1975 there was in excess of $96,000 worth of unreported travel agent ticket sales, which represents a minimum of $2,208,000 unpaid for transportation. There is no mention of this in the Coopers and Lybrand report or in the Clarkson, Gordon report. They did not touch on any of these matters at all, so that Mr. Cochrane's statement that they have had a real in depth audit made is absolute nonsense.
I have also pointed out that Air Canada's own internal auditors endeavoured to audit the refund bank drafts account in 1975. This account is not less than $2.5 million per month, about $30 million a year. They finally gave up, and this account remains unaudited since 1972. Therefore over the past four years a $120 million account has been in question. The Clarkson, Gordon statement in the Estey report makes no mention of that whatsoever.
I have also been pointing out that Air Canada has been writing off debts from corporations as large as $186,000. How can it allow a debt for air travel to accumulate to the amount of $186,000? It is rather obvious that these two firms have not been doing any detailed study whatsoever in the finance branch in Winnipeg. There is no mention of that in the Estey report or in the Coopers and Lybrand statement in the Air Canada report for 1975.
I have also pointed out in the past that Air Canada has been breaking IATA rules and regulations. They have issued bar vouchers for Tours Mount Royal to the tune of $27,384. All that Air Canada collected from this travel agent was $9,445; they wrote off $17,938. This is illegal under IATA rules and regulations and is another matter that the Auditor General should look at.

So, with respect to the problems of the Air Canada lockout I think it can be said-and the hon. member knows it; if he does not, he should-that a-

Departmental officials are keeping in close contact with this situation and every effort is being made to assist the parties in the resolution of this protracted and very involved dispute. Recently, on June 18, the minister sent a telegram to the President of the Canadian Airline Employees Association which reads as follows;
This is in reply to your telegram advising that you find Air Canada's action of June 16 inexcusable although you recognize the company has exercised its legal rights under the Canada Labour Code. You are aware the union acquired the right to strike and the employer the right to lockout on October 22, 1975.
