subtopic: ENERGY-PROPOSAL FOR LOCATION OF URANIUM PROCESSING PLANT IN SAKSATCHEWAN-PUBLIC PARTICIPATION IN SITE DECISION

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subtopic: ENERGY-PROPOSAL FOR LOCATION OF URANIUM PROCESSING PLANT IN SAKSATCHEWAN-PUBLIC PARTICIPATION IN SITE DECISION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I undertake to stick directly to the topic I raised in the House on June 17. You will recall that on that date I asked for an assurance from the minister through the parliamentary secretary, who was standing in the place of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie), that before a final decision is made on the establishment of an uranium processing plant there would in fact be a full public inquiry. The parliamentary secretary said in reply at that time that Eldorado Limited "when it does make a final decision as to the location of the refinery will have a full public information program". Today in the House the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources again argued for public education on the question of nuclear power. It is all important that those who might be most directly affected have the right to know the full circumstances of the proposal and to make their concerns known as well.
What I was trying to elicit from the parliamentary secretary was an assurance that before the decision is made there will in fact be a full opportunity for representation and a full opportunity for education.
I have had the opportunity of travelling in my constituency in the area which is now under consideration by Eldorado and the provincial government, and I have heard repeated expressions of concern that the decision will be made before an opportunity is given to the public for input, and also before a full explanation of some of the safety factors is given.
If nuclear power refining is as safe as the government maintains, we should have a full public inquiry so that the concerns of the citizens in the area can be laid to rest. As I said, there is to be substantial investment, as this is a capital intensive process. It is anticipated that something in the area of $50 million will be invested. This will be of great economic benefit to the area but, notwithstanding that fact, it is only fair to point out to the parliamentary secretary some of the concerns that are being expressed, and possibly he will take these under advisement and relate them to the minister and Eldorado.
First, before the decision is made hearings should take place. Secondly, only after the environmental impact assessment, which is undertaken by the federal Department of the Environment, is completed and has been made public should a decision be made. The hearings should not simply consider the site of the proposed plant, but whether the refinery plant should in fact be established in the province of Saskatchewan.
Some concerns have been expressed and I would hope that Eldorado, before making its final decision in respect of the location, would in fact deal with these concerns. The public education process should take place before the decision is made and not after.
In regard to the matter of safety, I think the people in the area should be satisfied before a decision is made whether they are getting involved in a situation that has been determined in advance over which there is some concern about safety considerations. These concerns have

June 21, 1976

been expressed to me as first being in respect of radiation. Any level of radiation is known to cause biological damage. Therefore setting "soft standards" can be somewhat arbitrary. Simply because radioactive material is emitted from an industrial source at a level that is safe does not mean that it cannot cause some harm. Apparently no solution has been found to the problem of long-term storage or disposal of the highly radioactive fission products from nuclear reactors. Then there is the question of possibility of theft of the product from the refining plant.
An explanation should be given to the public in respect of the whole area of possible accidents. The arguments of the industry about safety are predicated on a level of fail-safe technology, in the absence of human error, which has not been demonstrated in any other similar venture. The next question is in respect of opposition abroad. We have the example of the recent referendum in California. One third of the people there voted for a moratorium on the development of nuclear power. The people of California have had substantial experience with nuclear power, and I believe the number of people who expressed some concern is significant.
As I say these are the concerns which have been expressed. I simply bring this to the attention of the parliamentary secretary. With the experience of the Port Hope situation I want to know whether this is perceived as being a problem or whether this is a completely different situation. This should be made quite clear to the people in the proposed site area. I bring this to the attention of the parliamentary secretary so that these matters can be dealt with in advance of a decision rather than afterward.
There is also the question of health hazards to workers. I think this is an area which also should be fully explained by Eldorado so that people who might be employed in such a plant would be aware of the situation. Another very important consideration, I think, is the benefit to the province. I think this is an area of public information which should be entertained by the government. I realize this is a capital intensive project. Since there will be something in the area of between 150 and 200 employees it is not a labour intensive project.
These are my remarks and I simply ask for elucidation. What I am hoping to obtain from the parliamentary secretary is assurance that he will in fact undertake that there will be a public inquiry before the final decision is made in respect of the location. I hope he will be able to give an affirmative answer to that.

subtopic: ENERGY-PROPOSAL FOR LOCATION OF URANIUM PROCESSING PLANT IN SAKSATCHEWAN-PUBLIC PARTICIPATION IN SITE DECISION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in responding to the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar (Mr. Hnatyshyn) I want to assure him that there is considerable economic benefit to the province of Saskatchewan from the establishment of a uranium refinery and conversion facilities in that province. Indeed I do not believe the provincial government would allow this uranium, which is being mined in increasing quantities, to be refined outside the province if it were at all possible to prevent it. In that connection there has been full consultation between the Saskatchewan government and Eldorado Nuclear Limited. As a matter of fact there has been a great deal of consultation with Sedco and the Saskatchewan Scientific Council as well as the government Department of the Environment
Adjournment Debate
and other federal government agencies on this subject. At this stage they are evaluating several sites in the province to determine the best possible site from an economic point of view. That is one priority. A second priority is the environmental impact of the plant.
I should caution the hon. member that we are talking about a plant which I believe is to come on stream in the next four to six years. In fact the exact capacity of the plant is not known at this time because firm commitments for production from the new mines coming on stream in Saskatchewan have not been determined. In any event, when this has been decided, the plant will be the most modern possible. The company has indicated that when they get closer to a decision on the actual site preferred, they will have public consultation.
I believe that the environmental impact studies will also require public consultation. Surely it is desirable from every point of view to have as much information available to the people, expecially in the immediate area where the plant will be located. I will make representations to Eldorado to ask that there be good public consultation before a final decision is reached on the question of the location of the uranium refinery in Saskatchewan.

subtopic: THE CANADIAN ECONOMY-AREA IN WHICH JOBS WILL BE CREATED THIS YEAR
THE CANADIAN ECONOMY-AREA IN WHICH JOBS WILL BE CREATED THIS YEAR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the question that I am dealing with tonight is one which I put to the minister on May 26, the day following his non-budget. At that time I asked the minister if he could identify where the 250,000 jobs would be created in the current year, and lo and behold the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Chretien) helped out the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) by saying "In Canada", and then the Minister of Finance added that he thought there would be an opportunity during the course of the budget debate to get into this point more fully.
I pressed the matter, stating that there had been a suggestion of auxilliary work being created through such studies as the one carried out by the Economic Council of Canada and I asked whether the minister could be more specific, where exactly do they see the 250,000 jobs being created, is it mainly in the private sector, the government sector, or a bit of both; in short, have they make-work programs in mind?
In his second response the Minister of Finance passed it off to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras) and said he thought that that minister would deal with the question, again during the budgetary debate. Unfortunately no minister has dealt properly with this very vital question in Canada today. I think the most basic tragedy in the nation is the fact that we have some 700,000 people out of work. When you read the budget you find that the minister's own figures indicate that that may be aggravated this year in that it is likely that 300,000 jobs will be needed this year, and yet the budget contemplates the creation of only 250,000 jobs to satisfy those who will be looking for work.
14730

June 21, 1976
Adjournment Debate
Essentially the government's fundamental problem is that it cannot make up its mind if it intends to count on the private sector to produce the jobs that are needed in the country, or whether it must have public participation to create these jobs. Certainly our belief is that the private sector can produce if the government would renew the confidence that is essential in the private sector to get on with creating the jobs that are needed. This is something that we have emphasized time and time again, but unfortunately we find that the present administration's response is really in response to the problems that it itself creates, and it comes up with the solution that it must participate still further in creating the problem by, according to it, creating the solution.
This minister is very fond of referring us to the United States and of stating, as he did on May 26, that we must wait for world markets to upturn in order that, somehow or other, we can get up to a higher level of prosperity in this country. I would point out to the minister and his parliamentary secretary that the U.S. has in fact turned its economy around in a much more imaginative way than we have in Canada. It has done it essentially by counting on the private sector to produce the type of real growth to which I am referring tonight.
In short, I hope the parliamentary secretary will give us a further explanation as to what the government plans, not just for the immediate future, not just for between now and March 31 next, but what it plans for 1977 and 1978, to ensure that there will be a lower level of unemployment in this country than we see at the present time.
Having talked with some backbenchers on the government side, I believe that the hard fact is that they have no plans. They are drifting, and they are hoping, but that is not good enough. Other nations have shown, through imagination and through proper industrial strategy, that there are ways to create job opportunities and to relieve unemployment.
With the resources we have there is no reason to believe that we cannot do likewise, and certainly for the minister, in response to my question on May 26 and also in response to the questions of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark), to indicate that it is the export trade turn up upon which we are counting, and nothing else, is not satisfactory.
I would like to conclude now, and I hope that the parliamentary secretary will shed a light as to where in fact these 250,000 jobs are going to be created. If he cannot, we must assume that the minister himself had no idea of what he spoke on May 25.

Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) stated when he began his speech he did ask questions. I looked at the questions he
raised on May 26, and he is quite correct, he did ask questions, but I think he stopped short in looking at page 13845 because on the next page there were questions raised and answers given.
At the risk of being repetitious I should say that the hon. member should have paid attention to the speech which was given in this House by the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras) which regard to job creation, a subject with which he is very much concerned. I will try to be very brief, but I will be going over the same answers which were given, with possibly a little more detail.
In the section of the budget speech dealing with the international economy the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) pointed out that, and I quote:
The international economy is launched on recovery from the depths of the worst recession since the great depression of the 1930's. The output of the industrial nations making up the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development stagnated during 1974 and declined sharply at an over all annual rate of 5 per cent during the first half of last year. This decline, fortunately, was arrested by mid-year, and with the United States in the lead, the prospect for strengthening recovery seems well-assured.
As a result, one of the main sources of strength in the Canadian economy in 1976 will be our growth in exports. This growth will influence the gains in employment on an industrial and regional basis.
In terms of particular industries, we expect that the recovery in our exports will have a major impact on the goods-producing industries including manufacturing, mining and forestry. Both output and employment declined in these industries in 1975 as our exports feel sharply. Manufacturing employment should lead the way, followed by mining and forestry. However, the major portion of employment growth during the year will emanate, as usual, from the%services industries. Personal, business and community services industries will create the largest number of new jobs followed by wholesale and retail trade and transportation, communication and storage. Little growth is expected in the various levels of government employment during 1976.
In terms of the regional aspects, we expect all regions to benefit from the recovery. However, given the expected demand for our exports, strong output and employment growth should be registered in those areas which send goods to foreign markets. These include areas that export manufactured goods including automobiles and other durable goods, mining products including coal, and non-ferrous metals and forestry products including lumber, newsprint, pulp and paper.
